full_judgment:
Borhanuddin J : This appeal under section 48 of the Arbitration Act is directed against the judgment and order dated 21-6-2016 passed by the learned District Judge, Dhaka, in Arbitration Miscellaneous Case No. 476 of 2015 arising out of Arbitration Award dated 11-12-2014.

2. Brief facts are that the appellant and respondent herein entered into partnership business by executing notarized deed of partnership dated 5-2-2001 to set up a filling station under the name and style "M/s Diganta filling station" as dealer of Padma Oil Company, to buy and sale petroleum products and also for servicing and washing vehicles; Said partnership deed was supplemented by a supplementary deed of agreement dated 14-3-2001; Thereafter, both the parties executed a registered deed of partnership on 14-8-2001; It is stipulated in the deed that the nature of partnership shall be "At Will" with equal share, management of the business shall be run by the 2nd party-appellant and bank accounts will be operated under the signature of both parties. In the supplementary deed of agreement, it is stipulated, amongst others, that the respondent- 1st party will transfer half of the land out of total 11.71 katha wherein the filling station is established in favour of the 2nd party after final installment is paid to the Ministry of Works; In the registered deed of partnership, clause 6 reiterated that the 1st party will transfer half of the land in the name of 2nd party-appellant after doing necessary formalities and the Management of filling station shall be run by the 2nd party; Profit and loss will be divided equally; In clause 19 of the registered deed it is stipulated that all other matters not specifically provided in the partnership deed shall be guided by the partnership Act of Bangladesh keeping provision for arbitration in case of dispute or difference arise between the parties; Operation of the partnership business commenced in the year 2003; In course of business, dispute cropped up between the parties and as per deed of partnership both the parties gone to Arbitration.

3. Contention of the 1st party-respondent in a nut-shell is that respondent obtained lease of 11.71 katha land at Mirpur, Dhaka, from the Ministry of Works, Government of Bangladesh, for establishing CNG Petrol Pump vide registered deed dated 13-10-1998; Since the respondent did not have necessary fund, he entered into a partnership agreement with the appellant on 5-2-2001 for construction, establishment and running of a CNG petrol pump with equal share. It was stipulated in the agreement that the appellant i.e. 2nd party to the agreement shall be the managing partner and invest all necessary funds for construction of the petrol pump and running the business; It is also stipulated in the agreement that the respondent 1st party shall transfer half of the land in favour of the appellant 2nd party; Said deed of partnership dated 5-2-2001 has been supplemented by a supplementary deed of agreement dated 14-3-2001 executed by the parties; M/s. Diganto Filling Station was established and run as partnership firm pursuant to registered deed of partnership dated 14-8-2001. It is also contended that the appellant instead of investing own money for construction of the petrol pump, borrowed money in the name of the firm in breach of partnership agreement. Further contended that respondent repeatedly demands accounts and balance sheet of the business but the appellant did not respond; Respondent signed some blank cheques and kept those to the appellant; Instead of giving accounts of the business, appellant sought dissolution of the partnership business vide letter dated 22-3-2006; Respondent asked the appellant 2nd party to adjust bank liabilities and finalize the account but the 2nd party without adjusting account filed Title Suit No.407 of 2006 which was dismissed since registered partnership deed provides arbitration clause; Respondent-1st party instituted Arbitration Case No.668 of 2007 in the Court of learned District Judge, Dhaka, under section 12 of the Arbitration Act, 2001, for appointment of arbitrator to resolve the dispute; Pursuant to the order of learned District Judge dated 31-1-2008, an Arbitration Tribunal was constituted. Both the parties appeared before the Tribunal, submitted respective claims adducing oral and documentary evidence in support of their claims.

4. Appellant 2nd party filed counter-claim in the Tribunal denying 1st party's claim and contending interalia that the land of 11.71 katha allotted in favour of the respondent- 1st party by the Ministry of works determining value of the land at Taka 10,12,500 and the respondent 1st party deposited 1st installment of Taka 1,37,500 but rest of the amount was paid by the appellant 2nd party in 3 (three) installments with interest on the assurance of the 1st party that after obtaining possession on payment of all the installments, he will transfer half of the land in favour of the appellant 2nd party which is evident from the partnership agreements executed by the parties but the 1st party did not comply with the term of agreement; The appellant 2nd party claimed that respondent 1st party borrowed Taka 11,83,000 from the appellant 2nd party by signing vouchers from 28-7-2001 to 6-7-2002; The appellant 2nd party also claimed that he spent Taka 53,11,061 for establishing the petrol pump and Taka 4,95,947 to pay wages of the labourers at the time of construction and for obtaining explosive license, BSTI purpose and others; The appellant 2nd party paid Taka 20,00,000 to the respondent 1st party through cheques for payment of loan liability of the respondent to one Mohiuddin Milon and in that regard an agreement was signed; The appellant 2nd party invested working capital of Taka 9,84,398. In his statement of claim, the appellant 2nd party stated that as per agreement between the parties they availed loan from Arab Bangladesh Bank in the name of M/s Diganta Filling Station and the amount was shared by the parties; All the expenditures including land development cost, construction work, fittings and setting up machineries etc has been borne by the 2nd party appellant since the 1st party had no capability to invest; Claim of the respondent 1st party is fictitious and a ploy not to transfer half of the land in favour of the appellant 2nd party as stipulated in the partnership deed.

5. It appears from the award that the Arbitral Tribunal formulated two points for consideration. One is whether the 1st party's claim of different types of loss, loan of Diganta Filling Station, accounts furnished by the 2nd party are correct and other is whether 2nd party's claim that half of the land of Diganta Filling Station to be transferred to him by the 1st party is valid. After perusing relevant documents submitted by the parties and sthterrent of the witnesses, Tribunal arrived at a finding regarding claim of the respondent 1st party in the following manner:

"The 1st party, it is agreed, that the Diganta Filling Station was established by joint venture with 2nd party; and deed of agreement is there; but the 1st party has not filed any original documents, or any evidence from the bank as PW to prove his claim. Only photocopy of some evidences has been filed, and thus under the law of evidence such claims are not establish; and thus the arbitration body cannot settle such claim" (Sic).

And thereafter regarding claim of the 2nd party-appellant, Tribunal arrived at a finding:

"If we go to the partnership deeds we find that the Diganta Filling Station was formed as a partnership entity for doing the business as agreed upon in those deeds and these deeds are admitted deeds. The very fundamental question in forming this partnership business was to establish a petrol pump with others ancillary business and for that end Mr Kazi Jahangir agreed to give 50% of the Diganta Filling Station land to Mr Sajjadul Karim but we have seen earlier that Mr Syed Sajjadul Karim suo moto withdrew himself from the partnership business on 22-3-2006, he thus no longer remained to give his partner to the said business. Thus when he no longer remained a contributing partner Syed Sazzadul Karim claim any share of the land as per deed of agreement because this partnership deed admittedly gives rise to such right only when he is a partner. Therefore claim in respect of respondent 1st party's portion of land is in his favour has no merit". (Sic)

6. Having aggrieved by the award, the appellant 2nd party filed Arbitration Miscella-neous Case No. 476 of 2015 in the Court of learned District Judge, Dhaka, under section 42 of the Arbitration Act for setting aside the arbitral award dated 11-10-2014. After hearing the parties and perusing materials on record, learned District Judge dismissed the case vide judgment dated 21-6-2016.

7. Having aggrieved by and dissatisfied with the judgment and order, 2nd party-appellant moved before this court under section 48 of the Arbitration Act.

8. Mr Prabir Neogi, learned advocate appearing for the appellant submits that on plain reading of the Arbitral Award in question vis-a-vis clause 18 and 19 of the registered deed of partnership dated 14-8-2001 makes it clear that the arbitral award has dealt with dispute not contemplated by or not falling within the terms of the arbitration and contains decision on matters beyond the scope of the submission to arbitration and thus the award is liable to be set aside under section 43(1)(b)(i)(ii)(iii) and (iv) of the Arbitration Act. Continuing his argument, learned advocate submits that as per clause 18 of the partnership deed the scope of submission to arbitration would be dispute or difference with regard to the partnership business and not regarding dissolution of partnership, as such, the award is liable to be set aside. He also submits that though clause 19 of the partnership agreement dated 14-8-2001 stipulate that all other matters not specifically provided in the partnership deed shall be guided by the Partnership Act, 1932, but Arbitral Tribunal passed the award without following provisions of the Partnership Act, as such, the award is liable to be set aside. He again submits that obligation of the 1st party and right of the second party have been stipulated in an unambiguous expression in clause 6 of the registered deed of agreement and thus failure of the Arbitral Tribunal to appreciate clause 6 and for that matter the partnership deed as a whole in it's true perspective has resulted in dealing with dispute not contemplated by or not falling within the terms of the submission to arbitration and for that reason the arbitral award contains decision of matters beyond the scope of the submission to arbitration and thus it is apparent that the award is hit by section 43(1)(b) (i) and (ii) of the Arbitration Act since the Arbitral Tribunal has stepped outside law, and it having stepped outside the law, it has stepped outside the jurisdiction. In support of his submissions, learned advocate referred to the case of SN Kabir vs Fatema Begum, reported in 66 DLR (AD) 193, the case of Central Bank of India vs Hardford Fire Insurance Company, reported in AIR 1965 SC 1288. By referring sections 7 and section 43 of the Partnership Act, learned advocate submits that in view of the above provisions of law read with clause 19 of the deed of partnership it is clear that arbitral award is hit by sections 43(1)(a)(b) and 43(1)(b)(i)and (ii) of the Arbitration Act. In this respect, learned advocate cited the case of Karumuthi Thiagarajan Chettiar vs EM Muthappa Chettiar, reported in AIR 1961 SC 1225. He next submits that the essence of a Partnership "at will" is that it is open to either partner to dissolve the partnership by giving notice and, as such, 1st party's letter dated 22-3-2006 is in essence a notice of dissolution of partnership at will and non mention of section 43 in the notice is not fatal. In this score, learned advocate cited the case of Con. Md Hashmat Ali vs Bangladesh, reported in 47 DLR (AD) I. He further submits that under the rule of law, anything in breach of law governing a certain area is in conflict with the public policy and thus the arbitral award is hit by section 43(1)(b)(iii) of the Arbitration Act.

9. On the other hand, Mr Qumrul Haque Siddique learned advocate appearing for the respondent 1st party submits that appellant has miserably failed to formulate any ground in his application for setting aside the award under section 43 of the Arbitration Act and, as such, the appeal is liable to be dismissed. He also submits that power of the District Judge to set aside an arbitral award under section 42 is not unfettered rather the power is strictly confined and limited to the specific conditions and grounds and thus learned District Judge rightly pointed out that he cannot sit on the award as a court of appeal and also cannot reassess the findings arrived at by the Tribunal as such there is no scope in law to interfere with the decision given by the learned District Judge. He next submits that under section 48 of the Arbitration Act, power and jurisdiction of this Division is confined as set forth in section 43 of the Act and therefore this court is not permitted by law to examine any other point either of law or of fact in deciding the appeal and, as such, there is nothing to interfere with the impugned judgment.

10. Heard learned advocate for the appellant and the respondent. Perused the paper book, additional paper book and papers/documents contained therein as well as citations referred by learned advocate for the appellant.

11. We have perused the impugned judgment and order. Learned District Judge arrived at a finding that under the Arbitration Act, 2001, court of the District Judge is not a court of appeal or revision as such has no legal jurisdiction to examine the reasonableness or justification of an award made by the Arbitrators and the court of District Judge has been given jurisdiction to set aside an award if the same is hit by any provision as laid down in section 43 of the Arbitration Act, 2001.

12. Admittedly, both the parties executed partnership deeds admitting that the nature of their partnership is "partnership at will". Section 7 of the Partnerships Act defines "Partnership at Will" and section 43 of the Act deals with dissolution of the partnership at will. 13. For better appreciation, section 43 of the Partnership Act is reproduced below:

43. Dissolution by notice of Partner-ship at Will:

1) Where the partnership is at will, the firm may be dissolved by any partner giving notice in writing to all the other partners of his intention to dissolve the firm.

2) The firm is dissolved as from the date mentioned in the notice as the date of dissolution or, if no date is so mentioned, as from the date of the communication of the notice.

14. Both the parties gone to arbitration for settlement of accounts and submitted their respective claim in writing. It appears from the arbitral award that the tribunal formulated points for consideration "whether the 1st party's claim of different types of loss, the loan on Diganta Filling station, accounts furnished by the 2nd party, the balance sheet is how far correct and how far the 2nd party's claim of 50% of the land of Diganta filling station to be transferred to him by the 1st party is valid" (Sic). The Tribunal nullify claim of the 1st party-respondent on the ground that 1st party has not filed any original document or any evidence from the bank to prove his claim and some photocopy of the evidence has been filed by which the claim are not established under the law of evidence. To consider claim of the 2nd party, Tribunal arrived at a finding that since 2nd party-appellant suo mow withdrew from partnership business on 22-3-2006 he is no longer remains as a partner of the business and therefore his claim regarding half portion of the land bears no merit.

15. It is clear that the nature of partnership between the parties was "partnership at will" as per provision of section 7 of the Partnership Act. Section 43 of the Act provides manner of dissolution of partnership at will. Again section 48 of the Partnership Act lay out methods for settling accounts between the partners in the following way:

"48. Mode of Settlement of Accounts Between Partners: In settling the accounts of a firm after dissolution, the following rules shall, subject to agreement by the partners, be observed:

a) Lossess, including deficiencies of capital, shall be paid first out of profits, next out of capital, and, lastly, if necessary, by the partners individually in the proportions in which they were entitled to share profits.

b) The assets of the firm, including any sums contributed by the partners to make up deficiencies of capital, shall be applied in the following manner and order:

(i) in paying the debts of the firm to third parties:

(ii) in paying to each partner rateably what is due to him from the firm for advances as distinguished from capital;

(iii) in paying to each partner rateably what is due to him on account of capital: and

(iv) the residue, if any, shall be divided among the partners in the proportions in which they were entitled to share profits.

<u>16. Admittedly, both the parties gone to arbitration to settle the accounts claimed by them separately, not for the declaration whether the appellant 2nd party remains as a partner after seeking dissolution by letter dated 22-3-2006. The award passed by the arbitral tribunal is not only half hearted one but in true sense is not an award under the scheme of Arbitration Act. It is clear that the arbitral tribunal without determining the points formulated by it dealt with the matter beyond the scope of the submission to arbitration and stepped outside it's jurisdiction and thus stepped outside the law rendering the award hit by section 43(1)(b)(i)(ii) of the Arbitration Act. We are aware that claims of the parties cannot be examined in this jurisdiction. Such a course of action is not permissible in view of the fact that this court does not sit as a court of appeal to examine and reappreciate the evidence and facts of the record. But section 36 of the Arbitration Act provides that in a domestic arbitration the Arbitral Tribunal shall decide the dispute in accordance with the substantive law in force in Bangladesh. The role of the court in adjudging compliance by the Arbitral Tribunal to it's duty to decide according to the substantive law in the subject of such content. The position has been explained in the case of Videsh Sanchaa Nigam Ltd. vs Shapoorjit Pallomji & Co. Ltd, reported in 2007 (Suppl) Arb. LR 313. Relevant portion is reproduced below:</u>

<u>"It is true that section 28 (section 36 of our Act)  Arbitration Act, requires an Arbitral Tribunal adjudicating upon a matter of the present nature to decide the disputes in accordance with substantive law for the time being in force. If the substantive law is disregarded, a challenger would make out a case for interference. But if in applying the substantive law, the arbitral tribunal commits an error in its interpretation or application, unless the result shocks the court's conscience, the court will not embark on an exercise to correct the error committed by a forum which the parties preferred over the court in the first place. But it does not follow that the court presiding over the setting aside proceedings would merely see whether the substantive law was applied without seeking to ascertain law it was applied. It is here that the court's conscience comes into play so that a party who has been unconsciously dealt with in the reference may not be penalized merely because it choose a forum other than the court".</u>

17. An arbitration clause in an agreement provided that the arbitrator and umpire were relieved from all judicial formalities and might abstract from following the strict rules of law and they shall settle any dispute under the agreement according to an equitable rather than a strictly legal interpretation and that their decision should be final and not subject to an appeal. It was held that the arbitration must in general apply a fixed and reasonable system of law which primarily and ordinarily means law of the land and they cannot be allowed to apply some different system such as the view of the individual arbitrator or umpire on abstract justice or equitable principles. Section 2 in defining arbitration agreement, says that it must be about a dispute in respect of a defined legal relationship.

18. In view of the above, we find that the learned District Judge failed to consider that the arbitral award passed by the tribunal does not follow the relevant provisions of the Partnership Act when admittedly the partnership between the parties was "partnership at will" as such hit by section 43(1)(b)(i)(ii) and (iii) of the Arbitration Act.

19. Accordingly, the appeal is allowed.

20. Judgment and order dated 21-6-2016 passed by the learned District Judge in Arbitration Miscellaneous Case No. 476 of 2015 arising out of Arbitration Award dated 11-12-2014 is hereby set aside.

Send down lower court records alongwith a copy of this judgment to the Court concern at once.

End.

full_judgment:
In this revision Rule was issued calling upon the opposite parties to show cause as to why the impugned judgment and decree dated 7-3-2011 passed by the learned Joint District Judge, 3rd Court, Cumilla, in Title Appeal No. 338 of 2009 allowing appeal and thereby reversing the judgment and decree dated 27-8-2009 passed by the learned Assistant Judge, Burichong, Cumilla in Title Suit No. 1122 of 2008 decreeing the suit in preliminary form should not be set aside and/or pass such other or further order or orders as to this Court may seem fit and proper.

2. Facts relevant for disposal of this Role, in short, are that one Taherun Bibi predecessor of present petitioners, instituted Title Suit No. 1122 of 2008 in the Court of learned Assistant Judge, Burichong, Cumilla, against the opposite party for a decree of partition of the suit property stating inter alia that the properly originally belonged to one Ansar Ali and CS khatian Nos. 3 and 4 stand recorded in his name. Said Ansar Ali died leaving two sons Kala Mia and Afsaruddin, two daughters Karpurer Nessa and Taherun Bibi. Kala Mia, Afsaruddin and Karpurer Nessa died one after another leaving Taherun Bibi, predecessor of the original plaintiff in the aforesaid two khatians Taherun Bibi owned 88 decimals of land out of which she transferred 7 decimals of land from plot No. 772 to one Sufia Khatun Bibi, the defendant No. 18. Recently, the plaintiff came to know that, the predecessor of the defendant Nos. 1-8 fraudulently created SA khatian No. 4 and DP khatian No. 2826 in their names in respect of the suit property. Said SA and DP khatians are wrong and without any basis. Moreover, the property mentioned in schedule to the plaint never partitioned among the co-sharers by metes and bound for which the plaintiff once again requested the defendants to get the property partitioned amicably for convenience of the parties to enjoy, but they refused to do the same. Hence the present suit for partition.

3. The defendant Nos. 1-12 contested the suit by filing a joint written statement denying all the material allegations made in the plaint contending inter alia, that the suit is barred by limitation; bad for defect of parties and not maintainable in its present form. Further case of the defendants are that the suit property originally belonged to one Ansar Ali and the same along with other property was sold in auction on 25-3-1934 for arrear rents in Execution Case No. 2893 of 1936. In the said auction the properly was purchased by the decree-holder Abdul Hamid Khondakar and others. Thereafter, said Abdul Hamid Khondakar and others settled die property to Zuma Gaji, Siraj Mia and Ibrahim who executed and registered two separate kabuliyatnama in favour of Abdul Hamid Khondakar and others on 4-2-1942. Said Zuma Gaji died leaving defendant No. 1 who got 37 decimals of land in plot No. 762. SA khatian accordingly stands recorded in his name to the extent of 8 annas share and also in the name of Ibrahim Mia and Siraj Mia to the extent of 4 annas each. Subsequent DP khatian also stand recorded in their names. The defendants have been possessing the suit property by way of inheritance and by settlement from 1942. The plaintiff has no right, title and possession in the suit property, as such, the suit is liable to be dismissed.

4. The trial court trained five issues for determination of the dispute. In course of hearing the plaintiff examined three witnesses as PWs and the defendants examined two witnesses as DWs. Both the parties submitted some documents in support of their claim before the trial court which were duly marked as exhibits. The trial court upon hearing decreed the soil in preliminary form against the contesting defendants by its judgment and decree dated 27-8-2009.

5. Being aggrieved by and dissatisfied with the judgment and decree of the trial court, the plaintiff preferred Title Appeal No. 338 of 2009 filed by the learned Joint District Judge, Cumilla. Eventually, the said appeal was heard and disposed of by the Joint District Judge, Cumilla, on transfer who upon hearing allowed the appeal and set aside the judgment and decree of the trial court. At this juncture, the petitioner moved this Court by filing this revisional application under section 115(1) of the Code of Civil Procedure and obtained the present Rule and order of status quo.

6. Mr Sagir Anwar with Mr Gazi Md Mohsin, learned Advocates appearing for the petitioners submit that admittedly the property in question originally belonged to Ansar Ali. On die death of said Ansar Ali the property in question ultimately devolved upon Taherun Bibi as only heir. The dispute between contesting defendants is only in respect of plot No. 762 under CS khatian No. 4. The defendant Nos. 1-18 claim that the property covered by plot No. 762 was sold in auction in decree Execution Case Nos. 909 and 910 of 1938 on 25-3-1939 and the same was purchased by decree holder Abdul Hamid Khondaker and others. The said decree-holder, auction purchasers settled the property to Zuma Gaji, Ibrahim and Siraj Mia for which they executed and registered two separate kabuliyat deeds in favour of Abdul Hamid Khondakar and others on 24-2-1942 and 25-2-1942. The trial court as well as the appellate court concurrently found that the defendants could not produce any paper in support of auction sale of the property by producing any such proceedings and on that findings the trial court decreed the suit in preliminary form, but the appellate court though agreed with the findings and observations of the trial court that the defendants failed to submit any document regarding auction sale but held that the kabuliyat registered in the year 1942 is of 30 years old document.

7. Mr Sagir Anwar further submits that in any settlement by zaminder, documents must He executed by lessor and lessee both but in the instant suit the kabuliyat in question tire unilateral documents. As such, by the said kabuliyat the defendants did not acquire any title in the property. In support of his such contention he has referred to the case of Wazed Ali Sheikh vs Most Hazera Khatoon reported in 2008 BLD 215 and Md Nizamuddin vs Government of Bangladesh reported in 1985 BLD (AD) 235. He further submits that the defendants could not file any deed of settlement in their favour even a piece of rent receipt showing payment of rent by them to the zaminder at any point of time. As such, the settlement so far claimed by the defendants have got no basis at all. Further, he submits that the present: BS khatian also stands recorded in the name of the plaintiff pursuant to a decree passed in Land Survey Tribunal Case No. 1155 of 2013, It is also argued that the defendants could not substantiate their claim that the property of Ansar Ali was sold in auction in any proceedings by adducing any evidence both oral and documentary before the trial court.

8. Finally, he submits that the plaintiffs right from their predecessor Ansar Ali and then Taherun Bibi, continuously possessing the suit land, but the defendants all on a sudden claimed that the property acquired by them by kabuliyats of the year 1942 which never acted upon and show the day light. As such, the trial court rightly decreed the suit but the appellate court without considering evidences led by the plaintiffs on misconstruction of evidences and misconception of law allowed the appeal and dismissed the suit. He submits that while preparing himself for hearing of this revision found that the plaintiffs ought to have prayed for a declaration of their title in the property. But inadvertently it was omitted by the conducting lawyer for the petitioners for which the petitioners filed an application for amendment of the plaint, only to the extent of prayer portion and prays for allowing the application and to pass necessary order in this regard.

9. Mr Md Abdul Kader Bhuiyan, learned Advocate appearing for the opposite parties submits that in the recital of kabuliyat dated 24-2-1942 and 25-2-1942, it has been clearly mentioned that the property was auction purchased by Abdul Hamid Khondakar and others in Decree Execution Case No. 909 and 910 of the year 1938 and the suit property under plot No. 762 was settled by decree-holder auction-purchasers, Abdul Hamid Khondakar and others in favour of Zuma Gaji, Ibrahim and Siraj Mia who executed and registered two separate kabuliyatnama in favour of auction purchasers. Since then Zuma Gaji, thereafter, his heirs, Ibrahim and Siraj Mia have been possessing the suit land. Accordingly, SA khatian stand recorded in their names. Subsequently, DP khatian also stand recorded in the name of defendants which proves that said kabuliyat has been acted upon. After SAT Act came into force and abolition of zamindary system the government accepted the defendants and recognized them as tenants under the government. As such, the auction sale has been established and the auction purchaser settled the properly in favour of Zuma Gaji, Ibrahim and Siraj Mia has been proved.

10. He further submits that the trial court while decreeing the suit in preliminary form failed to consider those documents aged about more than 53 years, ignoring the provisions of section 90 of the Evidence Act but the appellate court while allowing the appeal rightly held that the deed of the defendants being more than 30 years old, such document being produced from proper custody section 90 of the Evidence Act has entitled the court to presume that it is a genuine document.

11. He further submits that before the appellate court, the appellant opposite party submitted a photocopy of the certified copy of suit register relating to Suit No. 2893 of 1936 and Decree Execution Case No. 910 of 1938 which proves that there was a proceeding in which the property in question was sold in auction. But for laches on the part of the learned Advocate for the appellant-opposite party, the said document was not brought into record by filing an application for additional evidence. He further submits that this Court can take judicial notice on the said document for ends of justice.

12. Finally, he submits that kabuliyat of the year 1942, subsequent SA khatian and DP khatian in the name of defendants amply established that the property in question was sold in auction and decree-holder auction purchaser, Abdul Hamid Khondakar and others subsequently, settled the properly in favour of Zuma Gaji, Ibrahim and Siraj Mia for which they executed two separate kabuliyatnama in favour of auction purchasers. All those documents established that the defendant-opposite party acquired indefeasible right, title and interest in the properly and they have been possessing the same since 1942. As such, the appellate court rightly allowed the appeal and dismissed the suit. In support of his such contention he has referred to the case of Nurul Hoq Bhuiyan vs Momtazul Islam reported in 67 DLR (AD) 51 and Md Nizamuddin vs Government of Bangladesh reported in 1985 BLD (AD) 233.

13. Heard the learned Advocates for the parties, have gone through the revisional application, plaint in suit, written statement, evidences led by the parties both oral and documentary available in the lower court records and judgment and decree of both the courts below.

14. It is admitted by both the parties that the property covered by plot No. 762 measuring 74 sataks recorded in the name of Ansar Ali in CS khatian No. 4. The plaintiff in suit claims that on the death of Ansar Ali and his son Kala Mia, Afsaruddin and daughter Karpurer Nessa, ultimately, the property devolved upon one Taherun Bibi. Said Taherun Bibi while in possession and enjoyment of the properly, she transferred 7 sataks of land to one Sufia Khatun Bibi by a registered deed timed 20-8-1949 with whom Taherun Bibi was in ejmali possession in the same plot. Said Sufia Khatun Bibi is defendant No. IS in the suit. It is also claimed by the plaintiffs that the property in question never sold in any auction and no notice was served upon their predecessor and there is no existence of such soil and execution case in the name of Ansar Ali or Taherun Bibi. Therefore, it is the obligation of the defendants to prove that the property covered by plot No. 762 was sold in auction in any decree execution case. The trial court as well as the appellate court held that the defendants though claim that the property was auction purchased by decree-holder Abdul Hamid Khondakar and others but could not produce any such proceedings before the court. But considering age of the registered kabuliyat, the appellate court held that the kabuliyat of the year 1942 are old registered deeds, as such, is admissible in evidence without any formal proof.

15. Both the parties to the proceeding, on candid, submit that there are some loopholes on the part of both the parties in conducting the suit. Learned Advocate for the petitioner submits that admittedly in plot No. 762 the defendants and the plaintiffs are not co-sharer, but in plot No. 772 the defendant No. 18 and the plaintiffs are co-sharers. Therefore, the suit for partition can only be maintained against the defendant No. 1.8 not against the defendant Nos. 1-17. It is also submitted that the plaintiffs ought to have prayed for declaration of title at least in respect of plot No. 762 which is claimed by the defendants by virtue of kabuliyat of the year 1942 and settlement in their favour by the owners Abdul Hamid Khondakar and others. In the situation, this Court finds that the plaint in suit has not been property framed seeking appropriate reliefs. Similarly, the defendants in suit admitted that the suit register of concern proceedings in which the property was sold in auction ought to have been filed before the trial court by the defendant. But they failed to do so, but filed a photocopy of certified copy of the register before the appellate court which was not properly presented by filing an application for taking additional evidence.

16. In this precarious situation, this Court finds that the trial court at the first instance believing case of the plaintiffs decreed the suit in its present form and the appellate court believing the documents of defendants allowed the appeal. From observations made by both the courts below, this Court is not satisfied that the dispute between the parties has been properly adjudicated in the absence of any prayer on the part of the plaintiffs for declaration of title in the property and for not filing the proper document on the part of the defendants in support of their claim of auction and acquiring title by settlement.

17. This Court also finds that both the parties did not file any rent receipts showing payment of rent to zaminder or to the government at any point of time. Only two kabuliyat has been filed by the defendants which are unilateral document and executed by them. Both the courts below remained silent on the points; whether by such kabuliyat the defendants acquired any title in the absence of any rent receipts showing payment of rent lo the lessor-zaminder or whether by a unilateral document of kabuliyat any tide passed in their favour. Therefore, this Court thinks it proper to send back the ease on remand to the trial court for fresh trial allowing both the parties to amend their pleadings suitably and to produce relevant document in support of their claim and adduce evidence if so advised.

18. In view of the above, this Court finds merits in the Rule calling for interference by this Court.

19. In the result, the Rule is made absolute, however, without any order as to costs.

20. The judgment and decree passed in Title Suit No. 1122 of 2008 dated 27-8-2009 and Title Appeal No. 338 of 2009 dated 7-3-2009 are hereby set-aside.

<u>21. The suit is sent back on remand to the trial court for fresh trial affording opportunity to the parties to amend their pleadings suitably and to adduce evidences both oral and documentary for proper adjudication of the mater in dispute and the trial court is also directed to dispose of the suit as early as possible considering antiquity of the same.</u>

22. The order of status quo shall continue till disposal of the suit.

Communicate a copy of this judgment to the court concerned and send down the lower court record at once.

End.

full_judgment:
Mirza Hussain Haider J. This civil appeal, by leave, is directed against the judgment and order dated 06.07.1998, passed by the High Court Division in Writ Petition No. 941 of 1989 making the Rule Nisi absolute and thereby releasing the property being Holding No. 24/4/ Pallabi, Mirpur, Dhaka from 'Ka' list prepared and published in Bangladesh Gazette dated 23.09.1986.

2. Facts giving rise to this civil appeal in short are:

3. That Mrs. Mohsina Khatoon, (vendor of the present respondent), by sale deed No. 663 executed on 28.12.66 and registered on 18.01.67, purchased the case property and on 18.01.67 she executed a general power of attorney in favour of the Managing Director, Eastern Housing Limited, giving him power to take loan from the House Building Finance Corporation ("HBFC") or from any other loan-giving agencies for construction of her house. Mohsina Kahtoon expended Tk. 4375/- but as the said amount was too meager she mortgaged her land to the "HBFC". Mohsina Kahtoon with her son, Md. Rafi, an Officer of Shadharan Bima Corporation, lived in the said house since 1968, and in 1971, during the war of liberation, she vacated the premises. In 1972 on her return she found that the writ petitioner is occupying the case property against which Mohsina Khatoon made representation to the Sub-Divisional Officer (south) Dhaka on 01.05.1972 for restoring her possession by evicting the writ petitioner. As Mohsina Khatoon could not get back her possession she offered to sale the case property to the writ petitioner and a bainapatra was executed on 11.06.1974. The writ petitioner, on different dates from 11.06.74 upto 03.06.78 (on six occasions), paid an amount of Tk. 25,000/- only out of the total consideration money which Mohsina Khatoon received by putting her signature. From the last part of November, 1979 Mohsina Khatoon became blind. As such she received Tk. 2000/- and Tk.3000/- on 12.12.79 and 07.06.80 by putting her left thumb impression. The writ petitioner after execution of the bainapatra was put into possession of the case property in part performance of the contract. A vigilant team of the Government visited the case holding in 1975 and claimed the property to be an abandoned property. The writ petitioner prayed for releasing the property but the Government did not give any reply to his representation.

4. The writ petition, thereafter, moved the Court of Settlement in Case No.467 of 1989 and, according to him, the case was dismissed as barred by limitation. Thereafter, the writ petitioner filed the instant writ petition and obtained Rule Nisi.

5. The Rule was opposed by the writ respondent government, contending inter alia that the property is an abandoned property within the meaning of P.O. No. 16 of 1972 as the original owner was not present in Bangladesh and never applied for release of her property after the promulgation of P.O. No. 16 of 1972. No application of the alleged son of the owner was ever received by the Government at any material point of time for release of the property. No agreement for sale was ever executed by the original owner with the writ petitioner and moreover the original owner was not present in Bangladesh to execute any deed of agreement with the writ petitioner. The alleged sale deed has been created by the writ petitioner which has not been executed by the original owner and moreover the alleged sale deed has been created in contravention of the provisions of law. The inclusion of the property in the gazette is lawful as the whereabouts of the original owner were not known and she lost control, management and supervision of the property in person and the owner was not a national of Bangladesh. The writ petitioner also accepted the demand note of the Government to pay rents and also rents to the Government as occupier of this abandoned property. Further, the Government asserted that on his own statement the writ petitioner admitted that the case property is an abandoned property because admittedly the original owner Mohsina Khatoon was not possessing the case land at the relevant time and from his own statement it is also apparent that according to him the title to the case holding is still lying with Mohsina Khatoon because the writ petitioner has not yet established his title on the basis of his so called bainapatra by getting a decree from a competent civil court. The case property by operation of law vested in the Government. That means the Government stepped into the shoes of the original owner of the case property and the writ petitioner, having no title to the same, cannot challenge the action of the Government. The writ petitioner is a third party and on his representation the property cannot be released.

6. A Division Bench of the High Court Division, upon hearing the parties and on perusal of the materials on record, made the Rule Nisi absolute by the impugned judgment and order dated 06.07.1998 and there-by directing the writ respondents to exclude holding No. 24/4, Pallabi, Mirpur, Dhaka, from the list of abandoned properties as published in the Gazette Notification dated 23.09.1986 purportedly under section 5(1)(a) of Ordinance No. 54/1985 within 3(three) months from the date of receipt of the order.

7. Being aggrieved by the aforesaid judgment and order of the High Court Division the writ respondent-Government moved this Division in Civil Petition for Leave to Appeal No. 1102 of 1998 and obtained leave giving rise to this appeal.

8. Mr. Ekramul Haque, the learned Deputy Attorney General appearing on behalf of the appellant-Government submits that the High Court Division erred in law in not taking into consideration the list prepared under Ordinance No. 54 of 1985, which carries a conclusive presumption that the property has been rightly enlisted as an abandoned properties; it also did not take into Consideration that the writ-petitioner (respondent herein) admitted that he occupied the said property illegally in 1972 and residing therein though subsequently he started paying rents as a lessee of the Government. Such admission of the writ petitioner justifies the presumption that the property has been rightly enlisted as an abandoned property. He also submits that the writ petitioner is an illegal occupier of the case property since 1972 and subsequently claiming the property by dint of a bainapatra, allegedly executed by the original owner Mohsina Khatoon and, as such, the High Court Division came to an erroneous conclusion that the property is an not abandoned property, without considering that mere bainapatra under no circumstances can be construed as a title document. He further submits that the original owner, Mrs. Mohsina Khatoon, having not co me forward to claim the property by filing an application under section 7 of Ordinance No. 54 of 1985 before the Court of Settlement within time for exclusion of the said property from such list or to return the same to her on the ground that the same is not an abandoned property and that being an alternative efficacious remedy, invoking writ jurisdiction under article 102 of the Constitution is not at all maintainable. He next submits that the writ petitioner not being the owner cannot acquire fundamental right by purchase of an abandoned property in 1984. Finally he submits that the application filed before the Court of Settlement being rejected as being barred the High Court Division cannot act as an appellate Court to determine the facts of its own. The High court Division under article 102 of the Constitution can interfere with the decision of the court of Settlement only if the writ petitioner could make out a case that the Court of Settlement acted without jurisdiction and made any finding upon no evidence or without considering any material evidence causing prejudice to the complaining party or that the Court of settlement acted malafide and in violation of natural justice. Thus he submits that the appeal be allowed for ends of justice.

9. No one appears nor any concise statement has been filed on behalf Of the writ petitioner-respondent.

10. On perusal of the materials on record it appears that admittedly the writ petitioner is not the owner of the property in question rather one Mrs. Mohsina Khatoon wife of late Md. Shafi, of Section No. 13, Block-13, Road No. 12, Line No. 6, Quarter No. 12, Mirpur, PS. Mirpur, Dacca, purchased the same on 28.12.1986 which the writ petitioner admits. It is further admitted that the said Mohsina Khatun obtained loan from the House Building Finance Corporation and constructed a building on the said plot where she along with her son lived from 1968. Thereafter during the war of liberation in 1971, she had to vacate the house for her safety. But after her return in 1972 she found her house was occupied by' the writ petitioner and as such she approached the Sub-Divisional Officer, Dhaka, for release of the house from the possession of the writ petitioner, an unauthorized person but having failed to get back the possession of the same she decided to sell the property. Thus she approached the writ petitioner, who, being the Government-servant, agreed to purchase the same at a consideration of TK. 45,000/=. Accordingly a bainapatra was executed on 11.06.1974 on payment of an advance amount of TK. 10,000/-. It further appears that the writ petitioner claims that he paid TK. 35,000/- to the "HBFC" on account of repaying the loan. Thereafter, Mrs. Mohsina Khatoon became almost blind.

<u>11. From the record it also appears that the writ petitioner admitted that the vigilant team of the Government visited the case property in 1975 to whom the writ petitioner produced the bainapatra and asserted that he had been living there in part performance of the con-tract but the vigilant team in the absence of proper title deed directed him to vacate the case property as he was possessing the same as an unauthorized occupant. Thus he was compelled to agree that he would stay there as a lessee of the government on payment of regular rents, and as such he started paying rents as a lessee of the said abandoned property. Subsequently the writ petitioner claimed that Mrs. Mohsina Khatoon executed a sale deed in his favour on 12.06.1981 and also executed a document for registration of the same before the Sadar Sub-Registrar, Dacca. Thus the writ petitioner claims that the prop-is not an abandoned property at all within the meaning of PO 16 as Mrs. Mohsina Khatoon was available in Bangladesh and she executed a sale deed in his favour and she is possessing the said property.</u>

12. From the above facts it is clear that till finalization of the list of abandoned properties in 1985 under Ordinance No. LW of 1985 Mrs. Mohsina Khatoon was not in the picture either as a possessor or as an owner. It is the writ petitioner, who, admittedly being an illegal occupant claimed to be the real owner of the property by dint of bainapatra and subsequently vide an unregistered transfer deed executed by Mrs. Mohsina Khatoon.

13. In the meantime in addition to President's Order (PO) 16 of 1972, which was initially applicable to all types of properties as defined in Article 2(5) of the said Oder, the government enacted Ordinance No. LIV of 1985 for the purpose of enlisting the abandoned buildings, exclusively for the residential building in Urban areas excluding in certain matter stated in that Ordinance. In pursuance of the said Ordinance the property in question has been enlisted as an abandoned building under section 5(1) of the said Ordinance No. 54 of 1985. Section 5(2) provides that the list published under section 5(1) shall be the conclusive evidence of the fact that the buildings included therein are abandoned properties and vested in the government as such.

14. On the other hand section 7 of the said Ordinance provides as follows:

"7.(1) Any person claiming any right or interest in any building which is included in any list published under section 5 may, within a period of one hundred and eight days from the date of publication of the list in the official gazette, make an application to the Court of Settlement for exclusion of the building from such list or return or restoration of the building to him or for any other relief on the ground that the building is not an abandoned property and has not vested in the Government under the President's Order or that his right or interest in the building has not been affected by the provisions of that Order  (2)………

15. So it is clear that unless the claimant/complainant can prove by filing application under section 7 of the said Ordinance of 1985 before the Court of Settlement within 180 days from the date of publication of such list in the official gazette for exclusion of the same from such list or return or restoration of the same to him on the ground that the building is not an abandoned building and has not vested in the government as the owner's whereabouts are known and she/he did not leave this country during the war of liberation and he/she is a citizen of Bangladesh, the presumption would be that the property is an abandoned property and vested in the government as Such. But in the present case, the writ petitioner could not prove either of the aforesaid qualifications to be the rightful owner of the said property though he moved the Court of Settlement in 1989 but the Court of Settlement found the application barred by limitation and, as such, it rejected the same. Then he moved the High Court Division under article 102 of the Constitution for redress.

16. The writ petitioner did not annex any document with the writ petition before the High Court Division to prove that Mrs. Mohsina Khatoon, the admitted owner, was very much available in Bangladesh during the war of liberation and/or till PO 16 was enacted. He also failed to produce any document that the whereabouts of Mrs. Mohsina Khatoon was very much known. When the writ petitioner failed to establish/prove the where about of Mrs. Mohsina Khatun, the real owner of the abandoned property in question were known to everybody during the war of liberation and she is a citizen of Bangladesh and she is in possession of the property, there is no illegality to treat the same as an abandoned property under the PO 16. Moreover on the face of admission of the writ petitioner that he is a lessee under the Government and he took lease admitting the same as an abandoned property the writ petitioner has no right to ask for release of the property to him as the rightful owner of the same. Moreover, under no circumstances he can claim that he is the owner of the property on the basis of an unregistered Bainapatra, in the absence of any valid title deed acquiring title before PO 16 of 1972 came into force or enlisting the same as an abandoned property As such, he has no fundamental right for which he could invoke article 102 of the constitution claiming violation of fundamental right.

<u>17. On the contrary the present appellant produced a good number of papers to show that after taking over the property and publishing the same in the "Ka" List the property has been leased out by the Government to different lessees on receipt of rents and lastly the same has been allotted to a widow of a freedom fighter who while residing there died in the said property and her successor, as a sub-sequent allottee, is in possession of the same. Hence we are of the view that the High Court Division did not consider either of the afore-mentioned aspects and exceeded its jurisdiction under article 102 of the Constitution to make the Rule Nisi absolute by the impugned judgment and order which is liable to be interfered with by this Court.</u>

18. Accordingly, we find substance in this appeal. Hence this civil appeal is allowed and, as such, the impugned judgment and order passed by the High Court Division is set aside, however, without any order as to cost.

End.

full_judgment:
Naima Haider, J: 1. In this application under Article 102 of the Constitution, Rule Nisi was issued in the following terms: Let a Rule Nisi be issued calling upon the respondents to show cause as to why the inclusion 7.50 decimals of land, Housing No. 1088/1 Mouza-Ibrahimpur, J.L. No. 269, C.S. Khatian No. 11, C.S. Plot No. 268, S.A. Khatian No. 8, S.A. Plot No. 268, R.S. Khatian No. 365, R.S. Plot No. 1106, Police Station-Kafrul, Dhaka Cantonment Area, Dhaka having been enlisted in “Ka” list of Abandoned Building published in Bangladesh Gazette dated 23.069.1986 under serial No. 12, page No. 9762(4) under the provision of Abandoned Building (Supplementary Provisions) Ordinance, 1985(Ordinance LIV of 1985) should not be declared to have been made without lawful authority and is of no legal effect and as such the case prosperity in question, shall not be excluded from the said list of Abandoned Building (as contained in Annexure-J) and/or pass such other or further order or orders as to this Court may seem fit and proper. 2. In this writ petition, the dispute arises out of inclusion of the property/land in question, measuring 7.50 decimals, in the Bangladesh Gazette on 23.09.1986. Through this Gazette, the Government treated the property in question as abandoned property under Section 5(1) (a) of The Abandoned Buildings (Supplementary Provisions) Ordinance 1985 (“the 1985 Ordinance”). 3. In the instant writ petition, the petitioners claim that they are the owners of the property in question. In support, the petitioners elaborately states, with supporting documents, how the property devolved in their favour. Essentially, the petitioners acquired the property in question after the death of their father Md. Shamsul Haque. Mr. Haque became the owner of the property further to a gift from one Md. Main Uddin. The petitioners’ father had been in possession of the property during his lifetime. The petitioners have been in possession after their father’s death. On the land/property in question, building was constructed after obtaining permission from RAJUK. The tax for the land/property was also paid to the Government regularly till 1421 B.S. The petitioners became aware of the inclusion of the property in the Bangladesh Gazette in 1422 B.S. when the tahsilder office refused to accept the rent on the plea that the property was declared abandoned property through the Bangladesh Gazette dated 23.09.1986. Being aggrieved by the inclusion, the petitioners moved this Division and obtained the instant Rule. 4. The learned Counsel for the petitioners, taking us through the writ petition and the documents annexed, submits that the petitioners and their predecessors were in possession of the property in question and therefore, treating the property as abandoned property was illegal. He further submits that the petitioners and the predecessors paid land taxes to the Government till 1422 BS and therefore, the property cannot be treated as abandoned property. He also submits that the record of rights is in favour of the petitioners, the petitioners constructed multi storied building on the land after obtaining permission from the regulators and therefore, the land in question cannot be treated as abandoned property. On these, among other counts, the learned Counsel submits that the Rule should be made absolute with appropriate direction upon the respondents. 5. The Rule is opposed by the respondent No.1. An Affidavit in Opposition was filed. The learned Counsel appearing for the respondent No.1, taking us through the Affidavit in Opposition submits that the property in question is abandoned property under P.O. 16 of 1972. The learned Counsel also submits that the writ is not maintainable as the petitioners did not agitate their grievance before alternative forum, being the Court of Settlement. The learned Counsel further submits that the instant writ petition gives rise to disputed questions of fact regarding the ownership of the property and therefore, this Division should not interfere. On these, among other counts, the learned Counsel submits that the Rule should be discharged. 6. We have heard the learned Counsels at length and perused the pleadings and the documents annexed. 7. In the event a property is treated as abandoned property, the person aggrieved is required to agitate the grievance before the Court of Settlement within a stipulated time. This is a statutory requirement. The issue is whether the petitioners ought to have or could have referred the dispute before the Court of Settlement. 8. Section 7 of the 1985 Ordinance gives opportunity to the persons claiming any right or interest in a property to apply to the Court of Settlement to exclude the particulars of the property from the list of abandoned property. However, such application is required to be filed within one hundred and eight days from the date of publication of the official Gazette. Admittedly the petitioners have not done so. The issue is whether this should bar to exercise of our supervisory jurisdiction under Article 102 of the Constitution. 9. Since Section 7 of the 1985 Ordinance provides an opportunity to apply to the Court of Settlement to exclude property from the list of abandoned property, the said provision also implies that the person must know of the inclusion. How else can he apply? Why else should he apply? The issue before us is whether the petitioners could be construed to have knowledge of the inclusion. We note from the documents annexed that the Government accepted land tax till 2015. Furthermore, RAJUK also issued permission for construction of multi storied building on the land in question. If the authorities treated the property as abandoned property, they would neither have accepted rent from the petitioners nor would have issued construction permit. Thus the petitioners had no reason to believe that the property in question was included in the list. By the time the petitioners realized that the property was included in the list, it became too late for the petitioners to avail the alternative remedy. The petitioners could not have agitated the grievance before the Court of Settlement. Furthermore, since the Court of Settlement had been specifically empowered by statute to exclude any property from the list of abandoned property, the petitioners could not have agitated their grievance before any other Court. This is set out in Section 6 of the 1985 Ordinance. Unless this Division interferes, the petitioners, who for bona fide reason did not agitate grievance before the Court of Settlement, would be without forum. This Division cannot permit this to happen. Accordingly, this Division is of the view that it should exercise jurisdiction over the matter. We therefore hold that in the present circumstances, that the writ petition is maintainable. 10. The property in question was listed in the Bangladesh Gazette under Section 5(1)(a) of the 1985 Ordinance. This is set out in the impugned notification (Annexure-J). Section 5(1)(a) of the 1985 Ordinance is set out below for ease of reference: “ 5(1) The Government shall, after the commencement of this Ordinance and before the 31st day of December, 1988, publish, from time to time in the official gazette- list of buildings the possession of which have been taken as abandoned property, under the President’s Order;

11. It is clear from the wordings of Section 5(1)(a) of the 1985 Ordinance that the Government must take possession of the property in question; this is a mandatory precondition for inclusion of a property in the list of abandoned property under Section 5(1)(a) of the 1985 Ordinance. This is also the consistent view of both Divisions of the Supreme Court of Bangladesh. The Hon’ble Appellate Division, in the case of Marzina Khatun vs Bangladesh [13 BLC (AD) 140] took the view that in certain circumstances, actual possession is not necessary; constructive possession would suffice. The issue before this Division is whether the Government took possession of the property in question, either actual or constructive. 12. This Division is of the view that in case of dispute, the Government must show that the possession of property has been taken by it. The onus is upon the Government because the Government has the relevant documents which would prove that it has taken possession. In the instant case, we note that land tax had been paid by the predecessor of the petitioners prior to inclusion of the property in the Bangladesh Gazette. This prima facie show that the Government did not take possession of the property in question. Had it been otherwise, the Government would not have accepted land tax from the predecessors of the petitioners. Furthermore, we also note that the Government accepted tax on the property till 2015. We also note that RAJUK issued permission for construction of multistoried building over the property in question. Therefore, there is a presumption of possession in favour of the petitioners and their predecessors. Now, the issue is whether the respondent No.1 provided any documents to controvert the presumption of possession in favour of the petitioners. In the Affidavit in Opposition, the respondent No.1 did not annex any document(s) which show that the Government took possession of the property in question. The respondent No.1 did not even make such assertion. We are therefore, inclined to hold that the petitioner has prima facie satisfied this Division of the continued possession of the property in question. 13. The learned Counsel for the respondent No.1 submits that the property in question is abandoned property within the meaning of P.O. 16 of 1972 and therefore, the property had been correctly included in the impugned Gazette. 14. The settled position of law is that two legislations dealing with the same subject matter should be interpreted harmoniously. The relevant legislations are P.O. 16 of 1972 and the 1985 Ordinance. Under P.O. 16 of 1972 a property can be regarded as abandoned property subject to certain conditions. Order 7 of P.O. 16 of 1972 contains the functions of the Government in respect of abandoned properties. Under P.O. 16 of 1972, the Government is required to take possession of abandoned properites. Section 5(1)(a) of the 1985 Ordinance is attracted if and only if the Government took possession of the property. So the attributable interpretation is that Section 5(1)(a) of the 1985 Ordinance can be applied if the possession has been taken by the Government under Order 7 of P.O. 1972. Order 18 of P.O. 16 of 1972 provides that the Government shall maintain a separate account for each abandoned property. P.O. 16 of 1972 also provides that Government shall impose fine on tress passers on abandoned property. In respect of the property in question, the respondents failed to show that the Government took possession in accordance with the provisions of P.O. 16 of 1972. The respondents also failed to show the account for the property in question. If the predecessors of the petitioners were infact unlawfully occupying the property in question, then the Government would have proceeded against them. No such evidence was shown. To the contrary, the petitioners have annexed documents which suggest that even in 1979, the predecessor of the petitioners was the owner on record of the property in question; even in 1979 the Government received land tax from the predecessor of the petitioners. Therefore, the only logical conclusion that this Division has arrived is that the property in question is not an abandoned property and the property was erroneously included in the impugned Gazette. 15. The learned Counsel further submits that there are disputed questions of facts. Accordingly, intervention is uncalled for. This argument is misconceived. The issue before this Division is whether the inclusion of the property in question in the impugned Gazette Notification was in accordance with law. As stated above, for the inclusion to be in accordance with law, the Government must take possession. The respondent No.1 despite having all the documents relating to this property, failed to produce a single document which shows that the Government took possession of the property in question, either actual or constructive. To the contrary, the petitioners have shown evidence of possession, pre 1986 as well as post 1986. Therefore, we are not entirely sure how a disputed issue arose in the given facts and circumstances. 16. In light of the above, we are inclined to hold that the inclusion of the property in question in the impugned Gazette Notification was illegal and without lawful authority. 17. This Division therefore, disposes the Rule. This Division holds that the property in question was wrongly treated as abandoned property through Bangladesh Gazette dated 23.09.1986. All executives, who are not impleaded in the instant writ petition, are directed not to treat the property in question as abandoned property. The writ respondents are directed to formally release the property in question (particulars are set out in Bangladesh Gazette dated 23.09.1986 in page 9764(2) under serial No. 12) from Bangladesh Gazette dated 23.09.1986 within 1 (one) month from the date of receipt of our Judgment and order without fail. (emphasis added) 18. With the aforesaid observation and directions, the Rule is disposed of without any order as to costs. 19. Communicate our Judgment and Order at once for immediate compliance. End.
