SHEIKH HASSAN ARIF, J. 

1. This appeal, at the instance of the defendant Nos.1 and 2 in Title Suit No. 14 of 2009, is directed against judgment and decree dated 14.02.2013 passed in the said title suit by the Second Court of Joint District Judge, Sunamgonj thereby decreeing the partition suit in favour of the plaintiff-respondent No.1.




2. Back Ground Facts:  2.1 Facts, relevant for the disposal of the appeal, are that the respondent No.1, as plaintiff, filed the said Title Suit No. 14 of 2009 before the Second Court of Joint District Judge, Sunamgonj seeking a decree of partition in respect of properties mentioned in the first schedule to the plaint and thereby seeking shaham in respect of .09 acre land out of the said first schedule land as mentioned in second schedule to the plaint.




2.2 The case of the plaintiff, in short, is that the property mentioned in the first schedule under S.A Plot No. 1890 and 1891, under S.A Khatian No. 315 along with other lands originally belonged to Gonga Charan Biswas. On his death, defendant Nos. 4-9 became owner of the said property by inheritance. That the said defendant Nos. 4-9, while in possession as owner, transferred .05 acre and .04 acre land under S.A Dag No. 1890 vide two registered kabala, namely Kabala No.4792 dated 01.12.1987 and Kabala No.4916 dated 07.12.1987. Thereafter, the said defendant Nos. 4-9 sold the remaining land under S.A Plot No. 1890, namely in total 27 decimal land, in favour of defendant Nos.1-3 vide different kabalas. That the land under S.A plot No. 1891 under S.A Khatian No. 315 along with other plots were also sold by defendant Nos. 4-9 in favour of defendant Nos. 1 and 2 vide different registered kabala. Accordingly, the said properties were recorded in the name of defendant Nos. 1-3 during revisional survey primarily under Tasdik Khatian No. 3048, under Plot No. 3098.




2.3 That upon proposal of marriage between the plaintiff and defendant No.3, as came through common relatives, the plaintiff and defendant No.3 got married to each other vide registered kabinnama dated 11.07.2005 with a fixed dower of Tk. 5,00,001. That out of the said fixed dower, Tk. 2,00,000/- was shown to be realized as against ornaments and furniture, Tk. 2,00,001 remained to be paid on demand. That, as against the remaining dower of Tk. 1,00,000/-, defendant No.1 (father of defendant No.3) transferred .09 acre land under S.A Plot No. 1890, as mentioned under second schedule to the plaint, by writing at Clause No.16 of the kabinnama. That in Clause No.11 of the kabinnama, defendant No.1 signed as a witness. That the said .09 acre land is under common possession of the plaintiff along with defendant Nos.1 and 3. That the plaintiff has not yet got the said Tk. 2,00,001/- as against the dower on demand. That while the plaintiff and defendant No.3 were in conjugal life, defendant No.3 left for England and stopped any communication with the plaintiff since February 2008. Under such circumstances, when the plaintiff contacted defendant No.1 (father of defendant No.3), defendant No.1 told the plaintiff that defendant No.3 would never take plaintiff to England. The plaintiff then demanded the remaining portion of the dower including the said .09 decimal land, which was refused by the defendant No.1. Under such circumstances, the plaintiff filed the said suit seeking saham in respect of the said .09 decimal land.




2.4 The suit was contested by defendant Nos.1 and 2 (parents of defendant No.3) denying the material statements in the plaint and thereby contending that the defendant No.1 never wrote anything on the kabinnama in question as regards transfer of the said .09 decimal land and that the kabinnama was registered even before solemnization of the marriage between the plaintiff and defendant No.3. That the defendant Nos. 1 and 2 purchased the said land along with other lands under S.A Plot No. 1890 and 1891 and they have muted 15 decimal land vide Mutation Case No. 84/ 90-91 and 11 decimal land vide Mutation Case No. 70/ 2007. That the suit land is the purchased land of these defendants and that they have residence thereon. That the defendant No.1 signed the kabinnama out of innocence and the kazi of the marriage in question was brought by the father of the plaintiff. That the defendant No.1 had already transferred .09 decimal land from other plot in favour of the plaintiff. That the statement at Clause No.16 in the kabinnama was written by the kazi concerned under the influence of the plaintiffs father as regards transfer of .09 decimal land under S.A Plot No. 1890 and that the defendant No.1 never transferred any such land through the said kabinnama.




2.5 Upon such contesting pleadings, the Court below framed issues in the following terms:

(1) Whether the suit is maintainable in its present form?

(2) Whether the suit suffers from defect of parties?

(3) Whether the plaintiffs have right, title, interest and possession in the suit land?

(4) Whether all properties have been brought into the common hotchpotch of the partition suit?

(5) Whether the plaintiff is entitled to get a preliminary decree of partition?




2.6 During trial, the plaintiff produced three witnesses (P.Ws. 1-3) and certain documentary evidences which were marked as Exhibits 1-5. On the other hand, the defendant No.1 deposed himself as D.W.1 and produced certain documentary evidences which were marked as Exhibits Ka-Cha series. Thereupon, the Court below, after hearing the parties, decreed the suit in favour of the plaintiff and, accordingly, gave saham of the said .09 decimal land mentioned in schedule 2 in favour of the plaintiff. Being aggrieved by such preliminary decree, the defendant Nos.1 and 2 have preferred this appeal, but have not sought any order of stay for staying operation of the judgment passed by the Court below.




2.7 The appeal is contested by plaintiff-respondent No.1 through learned advocate Mr. M. Ali Murtaja.




3. Submissions: 

3.1 Mr. Surojit Bhattacharjee, learned advocate appearing for the appellants, after placing the entire impugned judgment and the nikahnama in question, namely Exhibit-3, submits that the statement in Clause-16 of the kabinnama could not be proved by the plaintiffs before the Court below to be the statement of the defendant No.1 and as such, according to him, the Court below committed gross illegality in decreeing the suit and, thereby, giving saham in favour of the plaintiff in respect of the property mentioned in Clause 16 of the said kabinnama. He further submits that even if the statement at Clause No. 16 of the kabinnama is taken to be proved by the plaintiffs, the plaintiff cannot claim any saham in the property in question inasmuch as that such statement, even if made by defendant No.1, did not transfer any immovable property as per the provisions of Section 123 of the Transfer of Property Act, 1882. By referring to Exhibit-3 again, learned advocate for the appellants submits that the said statement in Clause- 16 of the kabinnama cannot be taken to be a contract for sale either, as any contract for sale of immovable property has to be registered in view of the mandatory provisions under Section 17A and 17B of the Registration Act, 1908, as amended by vide Act No. 25 of 2004.




3.2 Mr. Bhattacharjee further submits that in view of the provisions under Rule 19 of the Muslim Marriage and Divorce Registration Rules, 1975, the nikahnama is registered between two parties, namely husband and wife. Therefore, only these two parties may give commitment as regards dower. Therefore, according to him, even if it is found that the father of the husband, namely defendant No.1, who was a mere witness in the marriage, declared anything or transferred anything by way of the said kabinnama, such transfer cannot be implemented as because he was not a party to the marriage. He further submits that it is the husband who is responsible for anything as against dower and as such defendant No.1, being admittedly not the husband or party to the marriage, cannot be held responsible for payment of any dower or any portion of dower.




3.3 As against above submissions, Mr. M. Ali Murtaja, learned advocate appearing for the plaintiff-respondent, submits that anyone can give commitment on behalf of the husband to pay the dower money and, in this case, since the father of the husband, namely defendant No.1, declared transfer of the land in question in favour of the plaintiff as against the remaining portion of Tk. 1,00,000/- of the dower money, the Court below has rightly decreed the suit and thereby gave saham in respect of the said property in favour of the plaintiff.




4. Deliberations, Findings and Orders of the Court:

4.1 Some important questions with religious sensitivity have arisen in this appeal, namely:

(1)Whether the father of the husband may pay the dower money or may under-take to pay the dower money or portion of dower money on behalf of his son (husband) given that as per the law, namely Muslim Marriage and Divorces (Registration) Rules, 1975, he is not directly a party to such marriage?

(2) Whether on behalf of a party to the marriage, any person may undertake to transfer land instead of the dower money or what may be the form of dower?

(3) Whether such transfer of land by the father of the husband as against dower or portion of dower, as made at Clause 16 of the nikahnama, may be effected and enforced under the Muslim Law and the law of the land?




4.2 Considering such religious sensitivity and complex issue of law of the land, we have requested two Islamic scholars of Bangladesh Islami Foundation and a senior counsel of this Court to assist us as Amici Curiae. Accordingly, on our request, Mr. Mufti Md. Abdullah, Mufti Bangladesh Islamic Foundation, Baitul Mukarram, Dhaka and Dr. Md. Abu Saleh Patwary, Muffassir and Deputy Director, Bangladesh Islamic Foundation, Baitul Mokarram, Dhaka have provided assistance by their scholarly views through virtual connectivity. After their such assistance, Mr. A.F. Hassan Ariff, learned senior counsel, has also assisted us as Amicus Curiae to resolve the issue of law of the land as against such religious context. In addition to their oral submissions, both the above named Islamic Scholars have also submitted their opinion in writing.




4.3 It may be noted that the opinion of both the scholars were unanimous and we have not found any major difference in between their opinion. According to them, a dower may be in any form: cash, kind or in the form of property or any other valuables, and it is the right of the wife and obligation of the husband to pay or transfer the dower in favour of the wife at the time of marriage or thereafter. According to them, it is the dictate of Allah as well as Hazrat Muhammad (SM) that the dower must be paid by the husband and unless and until it is paid, it will remain as the loan or liability on the husband.




4.4 The said scholars have further stated unanimously that the liability to pay dower may be under-taken by the father, brother or any relatives or anyone else on behalf of the husband and it could be paid in the form of cash, valuables and land etc. The gist of their opinion is that any property or valuables, which are valid in Islam, may take the form of dower and anyone can undertake to pay or transfer such dower.




4.5 From the above opinion of the said islamic scholars, it appears that the landed property, being a valid property under Islam, may take the form of dower under Islamic principles, and anyone, including the father of the husband, may undertake to pay or transfer such dower. Therefore, it appears that the landed property in question was rightly taken to be a form of portion of dower to be transferred in favour of the plaintiff and that the father of the husband, namely defendant No.1, was allowed under the Islamic law to undertake or to transfer the said land in lieu of certain portion of the said dower money in favour of his daughter-in- law. Probably, considering this aspect of the Islamic principle, Clause-16 of the nikahnama has been incorporated in the standard nikanama form, which runs as follows:




"১৬।বিশেষ বিবরণ ও পক্ষগণের মধ্যে চুক্তিসুত্রে নির্ণীত মূল্যসহ কোন সম্পত্তি সম্পূর্ণ দেনমোহর বা উহার অংশ বিশেষের পরিবর্তে প্রদত্ত হইয়াছে কিনা?...........

১৭. বিশেষ শর্তাদী থাকিলে…………..”

4.6 Admittedly, the appellant (defendant No.1) signed the said nikahnama as a witness, although he is disputing the statement made by him under Clause No. 16. Now the question is even if he has made such statement as regards transfer of .09 decimal land in favour of the plaintiff, whether such transfer may be valid transfer under the law of the land.




4.7 The admitted position is that the nikahnama was registered on 11.07.2005, i.e., after the enforcement of the Amending Act No. 25 of 2004 thereby incorporating Sections 17A and 17B in the Registration Act, 1908. Therefore, according to Mr. A.F. Hasan Ariff, learned senior counsel, such transfer, being not registered under the Registration Act, 1908, would become void as per the said Act and Transfer of Property Act, 1882. According to him, such statement of defendant No.1 may also not be taken as a contract for sale of land, as, after such amendment, such contract of sale in respect of immovable property has to be registered mandatorily and in case of non-registration, such contract would become void. However, by referring to the provisions of the Family Court Ordinance (Ordinance No. 18 of 1985), in particular Sections 3 and 5 of the said Ordinance, he submits that the proper recourse, as should have been taken by the plaintiff, was to file a suit for dower before the Family Court.




4.8 In this regard, we have examined the provisions of the Family Court Ordinance, 1985. It appears from the relevant provisions of the said Ordinance that the same is a special law by which a special Court, namely Family Court, has been established and that the provisions of the said law have been given overriding effect over any other law found to be inconsistent. As per Section 5 of the said Ordinance, the jurisdiction of the Family Court has been conferred relating to or arising out of all or any of the following matters, namely (a) dissolution of marriage (b) restitution of conjugal rights (c) dower (d) maintenance (e) guardianship and custody of children. Therefore, it appears that a wife is entitled to file a suit claiming a decree of dower before the Family Court established under the Family Court Ordinance, 1985. The term 'dower' has not been defined either by the Muslim Family Law Ordinance, 1961 or by the Family Court Ordinance, 1985. However, Section 10 of the Muslim Family Law Ordinance, 1961 provides that where no details about mode of payment of dower are specified in the nikahnama for the marriage contract, the entire amount of dower shall be presumed to be payable on demand.




4.9 Now, in Exhibit 3, namely the nikahnama in question, the mode of payment of dower has been stated clearly, namely that the total dower money is Tk. 5,00,001/- and Tk. 2,00,001/- out of the said Tk. 5,00,001/- was determined as the dower on demand and Tk. 2,00,000/-was determined as portion of dower money realized as against ornaments and furniture. At Clause-16 of the said nikahnama (Exhibit 3), a statement is claimed to have been made by the defendant No.1 (father of the husband), who has admittedly signed the nikahnama as a witness, as regards transfer of 9 decimal land. The entire clause-16 in exhibit-3 along with the said statement is quoted below:

“১৬। বিশেষ বিবরণ ও পক্ষগণের মধ্যে চুক্তিসূত্রে নির্নীত মূল্যসহ কোন সম্পত্তি সম্পূর্ণ দেনমোহর বা উহার অংশ বিশেষের পরিবর্তে প্রদত্ত হইয়াছে কিনা? বাবত নং ১০০০০০০/= (স্টেশন সাব রেজিস্ট্রার দিরাই-সুনামগঞ্জ। আমি ছদরুল হক, আমার খরিদা দলিল নং-৪৭৯২ তাং ১/১২/৮৭ইং ও দলিল নং ৪৯১৬ তাং ৭/১২/৮৭ইং মোট পরিমান (৫+৪)=৯ নয় শতাংশ জায়গা, থানা- দিরাই, জেলা-সুনামগঞ্জ, মৌজা- চান্দপুর, জে, এল, নং ৯৯, খতিয়ান নং সাবেক-৩১৫, ডি.পি. খতিয়ান-৬২৮ সাবেক দাগ-১৮৯০ বর্তমান দাগ-৩০৯৮ বাড়ী রকম ভুমি আমার পুত্র বধুকে দিলাম।”

4.10 Therefore, as per Clause 16 of the said nikahnama, it appears that the father of the husband has transferred the said .09 decimal land, as mentioned in the schedule-2 to the plaint, in favour of the plaintiff. However, the admitted position is that this nikahnama, though registered under the Muslim Marriage and Divorce (Registration) Act and Rules made thereunder, it has not been registered as per the provisions of Registration Act, 1908 and the transfer has not been made as per the provisions of Transfer of Property Act, 1882. Therefore, such transfer has become void in so far as the Registration Act, 1908 and the relevant provisions of the Transfer of Property Act, 1882 are concerned. Does it mean that the plaintiff does not have any remedy as against the said dower money of Tk. 1,00,000/- in payment of which her father-in-law, namely defendant No.1, transferred certain portion of land in her favour?




4.11 As stated above, as per the opinion of the aforementioned Islamic scholars, such transfer of land is valid dower as per Islamic principle. However, since the land in question is the portion of dower as paid or purportedly transferred in favour of the plaintiff by the father of her husband, this Court is of the view that the forum as chosen by the plaintiff to realize such dower was not the correct forum under the law of the land. As our country has special law, namely Family Court Ordinance, 1985, the provisions of which will have effect irrespective of any contrary provisions in any other law including the Registration Act, 1908 and the Transfer of Property Act, 1882, the plaintiff should have taken recourse to the provisions of the said special law and should have filed a suit for dower under the provisions of the said Ordinance before the Family Court established under Section 4 of the said Ordinance.




4.12 In this regard, we have also examined the decision of a single bench of this Court as relied upon by the Court below in decreeing the suit, namely the decision of this Court in Altab Hossain vs. Aziza Begum, 17 BLC (2012) -71. In the said case, this Court opined that the plaintiff therein could have filed suit for partition seeking saham in respect of total quantity of the property as given by her late husband by the said registered kabinnama as portion of dower. However, transfer in question in that case by way of a registered kabinnama was done on 14.08.1975 i.e. long before coming into force of the aforementioned amendment to the Registration Act and Transfer of Property Act vide Act No. 25 of 2004. Since the newly incorporated provisions under Section 17A and 17B of the Registration Act and the newly incorporated provisions in the Transfer of Property Act did not have existence at that time, or were not considered in the said case, we are of the view that the decision therein is not applicable in the facts and circumstances of the present case.




4.13 Since the plaintiff in the present case has chosen a wrong forum, namely filed a partition suit before a civil Court having territorial jurisdiction, we are of the view that the plaintiff should be given a chance to withdraw the said suit at this appellate stage to file the same before the Family Court, as established by the Family Court Ordinance, 1985, for seeking a decree of dower in respect of the said property. Since we have already held that the land in question can be treated as dower, we are of the view that the plaintiff should be allowed to withdraw the suit at this appellate stage with a permission to file the same before the correct forum, namely the Family Court established under the Family Court Ordinance, 1985. Since learned advocate appearing for the plaintiff-respondent No.1, in the course of hearing, has made such prayer, we hold that this Court should allow the plaintiff to withdraw the suit with a permission to institute a fresh suit seeking decree of dower in respect of the said land, as mentioned in schedule 2 to the plaint, before the competent Court, namely the Family Court established under Family Court Ordinance, 1985.




4.14 Accordingly, the impugned judgment and decree are hereby set-aside. Let the suit filed by the plaintiff-respondent No.1 be withdrawn. The plaintiff-respondent No. 1 is permitted to file a fresh suit within a period of 04 (four) months from receipt of the copy of this judgment in respect of the same land, as mentioned in schedule -2 to the plaint, seeking a decree of dower before the Family Court concerned under the Family Court Ordinance, 1985. 5. With the above orders, observation, and directions, the appeal is disposed of. 6. Before we depart, we express our gratitudes to the aforementioned Islamic scholars and learned senior counsel, who appeared as Amici-Curiae before this Court and assisted us to reach a proper decision. Communicate this.




Send down the Lower Court Records.




I agree.

(Sheikh Hassan Arif,J)

full_judgment:
Abu Bakar Siddiquee J. This civil appeal, by leave, is directed against the judgment and decree dated the 14th day of February, 2012 passed by the High Court Division in Civil Revision No.2465 of 2006 discharging the Rule. 

2. The facts of the case, in short, are that the present appellant as pre-emptor filed Miscellaneous Case No.1 of 1995 on 19.01.1995 in the then 2nd Court of Sub-ordinate Judge, Patuakhali under section 24 of the Non-Agricultural Tenancy Act, 1949 for pre-emption with respect of 57 decimals land described in the schedule of the application for pre-emption and eventually, the case was transferred as Miscellaneous Case N.08 of 1998 to the Court, of the then Sub-ordinate Judge, Artha Rin Adalat Patuakhali. 

3. The case of the pre-emptor, in short, is that 4.86 acres of land of Plot Nos.4683/4684/4686/4694/4695/4707/47 43/4748/488614751/4725 of S.A. Khatian No.1380 originally belonged to Behari Lal, Chandra Kanta Saha and Bashanta Kumar Saha to the extent of six annas two gondas two karas, eight annas and one anna seventeen gondas two karas share respectively. Chandra Kanta Saha died leaving behind 3 sons China Ranjan, Nitya Ranjan and Sukhu Ranjan Saha. Sulchu Ranjan Saha sold his share to Nitya Ranjan by kabala dated 09.03.1983 who sold two decimals land along with other lands to the pre-emptor and A. Sobhan, A. Khalque and A. Kader. Chitta Ranjan sold equal quantity of land to the pre-emptor and the aforesaid three persons, Abdul Khaleque and Abdul Kader sold their share to the pre-emptor by kabala dated 31.07.1985. Chatta Ranjan Saha and Nitya Ranjan Saha by two kabalas 07.07.1983 sold their shares to Md. Eunus Hawlader and Fazlul Huq who sold their purchased land to the pre-emptor by two kabalas dated 03.03.1987. Aforesaid Abdus Sobhan sold his interest on 13.02.1993 to the pre-emptor and Nitya Ranjan Saha sold 14 decimals land on 05.08.1993 to the pre-emptor and thus, the pre-emptor is a co-sharer by purchase of each plot of S.A. Khatian No. 1380. Most Taherunnessa and other sold 57 decimal land from the above khatian on 26.05.1984 and 27.05.1984 measuring an area of 28'/2 plus 281/2 decimals in tota1.57 decimals land to Md. Haider Parvez, opposite party No.05 who possessed the same by constructing a house thereon. Haider Parvez by a kabala dated 08.01.1995 sold his 57 decimals land along with structure to pre-emptee Nos.1- 4 who are strangers showing higher value at Tk.3,00,000/- only. But to avoid complication, the pre-emptor deposited the entire consideration money along with statutory compensation as shown in the deed with a claim for returning back Tk. 1,00,000/- if the pre-emptees failed prove that actually Tk.4,00,000/- was paid. The pre-emptor has possessed the adjacent land of each side of the case land. The pre-emptor urgently needed the case land, that the impugned sale was held beyond the knowledge of the pre-emptor. If the pre-emptor was tendered or could learn before the transfer then certainly he would have purchased the same that the pre-emptor had no good relation with the vendor. The pre-emptor came to know about the transfer on 10.01.1995 and have filed the case on 30.01.1995 by depositing the consideration money as shown in the deed along with statutory compensation. 

4. Opposite party Nos.1-4 contested the case by filing written objection all the material allegations made in the application and contended, inter alia, that the pre-emptor has no locus standi to file the pre-emption application. The pre-emptor sustained no loss and injury by the impugned kabala, that the case land is situated in a compact block within pucca boundary wall that the pre-emptor has no land beside it. The pre-emptor has no necessity of the case land. The case is filed at the instance and ill advice of one Jalal Ahmed. The pre-emptor married twice and he has been lying in America with his first wife from a long time. The actual price of the sale was TK.9,00,000/- out of which 4 lace was for the land and the rest five lacs for the building which was written in a separate deed. The pre-emptor's case suffers from short deposit. The pre-emptor was a good friend of the vendor who recommended for transfer to the pre-emptees and he had previous knowledge about the transfer, that the scribe, identifier and attesting witnesses of the impugned deed are party men of the pre-emptor. There is a building consisting of 8 rooms in the case land, the case land was demarcated with the consent of the co-sharers and the land of plot Nos.4687/4688 are situated to the north of the case land which belonged to one Lutfunahar Begum. It is to the east of Pourasava Road and to the west there is the land of Mir Tazem Ali. The vendor opened a separate holding in the Pourasava and electricity connection was installed therein. A separate new Khatian with the consent of the co-sharers being khatian No.1380/6 was opened in Misc. Case No.90pk/1984 and order dated 26.11.1994. The vendor firstly mutated nature Case No.15PK11985-86. The pre-emptees incurred Tk. 1,05,000/- as development cost. There was a Bainapatra with the Vendor dated 14.12.1994 of that day Tk. 1,00,000/- was paid on 08.01.1995 out of which Tk.1,90,000/- by cash and Tk.5,55,000/- was paid through cheque. 

5. At the trial, both the parties adduced evidence. The trial Court by the order dated 20.06.2002 dismissed the case. 

6. Against the order of the trial Court, the pre-emptor filed Miscellaneous Appeal No.39 of 2002 before the District Judge, Patuakhali who sent the appeal to the Special District Judge. The Special District Judge, Patuakhali after hearing the appeal by the judgment and order dated 20.04.2006 dismissed the appeal and affirmed the order of the trial Court. 

7. Against the judgment and order of affirmance, the pre-emptor again filed Civil Revision No.2465 of 2006 before the High Court Division. A learned Judge of the Single Bench of the High Court Division by the impugned judgment and order discharged the Rule. 

8. Against the said judgment and order of the High Court Division, the pre-emptor filed Civil Petition for Leave to Appeal No.620 of 2014 and leave was granted to consider the following submissions of the learned Advocate for the petitioners: 
"I. For that the High Court Division has committed an error of law in not considering that S.A Khatian No.1380 is mentioned in the schedule of the disputed deed dated 08.01.1995 and the said fact was admitted by both the parties but erroneously held that the pre- emptor appellant has lost his right of pre-emption by separation of joint holding vide separate Khatian No.1380/6 in the name of respondent No.5 which has supposed to be subsequent creation after filing of the instant miscellaneous case and therefore, the impugned order passed by the High Court Division is liable to be set aside.
II. For that the High Court Division has committed an error of law in observing that separation of the joint holding, the other co-sharers ceased to be co-sharers and they have lost their right of preemption without considering that admittedly no notice was served upon the co-sharer in a mutation proceedings of the disputed jama and as such, order of sub division of the tenancy will be bad and not be binding on the non-notified co-sharer tenants and therefore, the pre-emptor did not cease to be co-sharer in the joint tenancy and as such, the impugned order is liable to be set aside."

9. Mrs. Nahid Yeasmin, learned Advocate, appearing on behalf of the appellant, submits that the learned Judge of the Single Bench of the High Court Division has committed an error of law in not considering that S.A Khatian No.1380 is mentioned in the schedule of the disputed deed dated 08.01.1995 and the said fact was admitted by both the parties but erroneously held that the pre-emptor appellant has lost his right of preemption by separation of joint holding vide separate Khatian No.1380/6 in the name of respondent No.5 which has supposed to be subsequent creation after filing of the instant miscellaneous pre-emption case and therefore, the impugned order passed by the High Court Division is liable to be set aside. She further submits that the High Court Division has committed an error of law in observing that separation of the joint holding, the other co-sharers ceased to be co-sharers and they have lost their right of pre-emption without considering that admittedly no notice was served upon the co-sharer in a mutation proceedings of the disputed jama and as such, order of sub-division of the tenancy will be bad and not be binding on the non-notified co-sharer tenants and therefore, the pre-emptor did not cease to be co-sharer in the joint tenancy and as such, the impugned order is liable to be set aside. 

10. Mr. Probir Neogi, learned Senior Advocate, appearing for respondent Nos.1(a)-1(c) made submissions in support of the impugned judgment and order of the High Court Division. He also argued that the pre-emptor and his family member left this country for America and the notice for separation of holding served upon his last destination. He further argued that since the suit holding has been separated by creating a new holding through a mutation case before filing of this case, the pre-emptors are no longer a co-share in the suit holding and as such the pre-emptor has got no locus standi to file this pre-emption case. 

11. We have considered the submissions of the learned Advocates for the parties concerned, perused the impugned judgment and order of the High Court Division and other connected papers on record. 

12. In the instant pre-emption petition, it appears that the disputed land measuring on area 0.57 acre appertaining to S.A Khatian No.1380 has been recorded as nul land but since the same has been fallen in the Patuakhali Pouro Area, the same is to be treated as Non-Agricultural land. 

13. It is admitted that no notice under section 23 has been served upon the co-sharer before execution and registration of disputed kabala. The appellant pre-emption has come with allegation that since no notice has been served under section 23 of the Non-Agricultural Tenancy Act, in such a position there is scope to ascertain the actual value of the land in question under section 24 (6) of the said Act. The petitioner has come with allegation that although disputed land has been sold at Tk.4,00,000.00 (Four lac) as has been shown in recital of the case kabala but actual value of the same is Tk.3,00,000.00/- (Three lac) only and as such, he is entitled to return back taka one lac. The contesting respondent-opposite party denied the aforesaid contention of the appellant-petitioner and counter claims that there is a building situated on the case land and the actual value of the land is Tk.4,00,000.00 (Four lac) and actual value of the building is Tk.5,00,000.00 (Five lac) respondent-opposite party appended a separate bainapatra and receipt of sale with the registered kabala showing actual value of the building. In this respect, opposite party No.1 Kazi Shajahan, deposed that the value of land has been shown as Tk.4,00,000.00 (Four lac) as has been shown in the recital of the registered case kabala and three is another un-registered document from which it can be seen that the value of the building has been settled and shown at Tk.5,00,000.00 (Five lac) in the PW2, Md. Hyder Parvez in course of his cross-examination admits that the value of land and building has been settled together. There was no embargo to insert the value of the land and building together in the disputed case kabala. Instead of showing the value of the building in the kabala, the respondent (opposite party) same forward before the Court with an unregistered bainapatra for proving the fact that building thereon also being sold to them. The learned Advocate appearing on behalf of the appellant termed the un-registered bainapatra in respect of the building as a subsequent creation with a view to frustrate the right of pre-emption. The verdict of a pre-emption case is an order. While deciding an application for preemption, the Court cannot go behind the intentions of the parties in executing the deed of the transfer. Any evidence to vary the terms of such deed is barred under the provisions of section 91 of the Evidence Act. On the basis of aforementioned proposition, the learned trial Court as well as the appellate Court being the last Court of fact has concurrently found that there is no justification to put reliance on un-registered bainapatra which alleged to have created subsequently. Both the Courts below also decided that the value of both the land and building amounting Tk.4,00,000.00 (Four lac) as has, been shown in the recital of the registered case kabala is the actual value. They also disbelieved the fact that the value of land and building was Tk.3,00,000.00 (Three lac) as has been claim by the appellant-pre-emptor is unbelievable since the recital of case kabala shows that the consideration of the same is TK.4,00,000/-. The learned Judge of the Single Bench of the High Court Division also approved such finding and decision. We find no illegality and inherent infirmity in the same. 

14. The respondent-opposite party has come with a further allegation that appellant-pre-emptor was a co-sharer in SA Khatian No.1380 but before execution and registration case kabala the disputed jama has been separated through a mutation case and a new Khatian being No.1380/6 has been created and as such, their co-sharership has been ceased and as such, they have lost the right of pre-emption. On perusal of the materials on record, it appears that in the present case, the vendor of the opposite party No.5 was Tahenumessa. She along with others purchased five annas eight gonads and three karas share from the recorded tenant Behari Lal who was the owner of six annas two gondas two kara share. She along with others on 28.12.1983 mutated their jama by filing mutation Case No.605 PK of 1983-84. After separation of holding the other co-sharers ceased to be co-sharers and as such, the pre-emptors have lost their right of pre-emption. On the other hand, he along with Abdus Sabhan mutated his name on 14.08.1986 in mutation Case No.83 PK of 1986-87 and separate Khatian has been prepared in their names. All these facts have been clearly noted S.A. Khatian No. 1380 which has been marked Ext. No.4 by the trial Court. 

15. Opposite party No.5, Md. Hyder Parvez, after purchase from Taherunnessa, mutated his name on 14.07.1985 through Mutation Case No.15 PK of 1985-86 and separate Khatian No.1380/6 was prepared in his name. It does not mean that the jama has not been separated and all the co-sharers of SA Khatian No.1380 are entitled to get notice of this mutation proceeding. The jama has already been separated through the mutation case. So, this pre-emptor petitioner has no scope to challenge the mutation proceeding of opposite party No.5, Md. Ryder Parvez. It further appears from the deed of the petitioner, it is clear that he has purchased the land from Plot No.4679 but not from the case Plot No.4686. 

16. The learned Advocate for the appellant (pre-emptor) has argued that the High Court Division has committed an error of law in observing that separation of the joint holding the other co-sharers ceased to be co-sharers and they have lost their right of pre-emption but without considering that admittedly no notice was served upon the co-sharer in a mutation proceeding of the disputed jama and as such, the order of sub-division of the tenancy will be bad and not be binding on the non-notified co-sharer tenants and therefore, the pre-emptor cannot be ceased to be co-sharer in the joint tenancy and as such, the impugned order is liable to be set aside. 

17. On the other hand, the learned Advocate, appearing on behalf of the respondent (opposite party) argued that the seller opposite party No.5 Md. Hyder Parvez after nurchase from Taherunnessa mutated his name on 14.07.1985 in Mutation Case No.15 PK of 1985-86 and separated Khatian No.1380/6 in his name and as such, the jama has been separated and all the co-sharers of SA Khatian No.1380 are entitled to get notice of this mutation proceeding and since the jama has alreadz been separated in the above mutation case, this pre-emptor has no scope to challenge the mutation proceeding of opposite party No.5, Md. Hyder Parvez, further from the deed of the petitioner, it is clear that he has purchased the land from Plot No.4679 but not from the case Plot No.4686 and thus, this appeal is liable to be dismissed. 

18. The learned Judge of the appellate Court being the last Court of fact has observed in the follows verbatim: - 
“উক্ত আইনের ২৪ ধারার বিধানে পার্শ্ববর্তী জমির সুযোগ নাই। ১নং সাক্ষী জেরায় স্বীকার করেন এবং ইহাও স্বীকৃত যে, মজহর স্বপরিবারে স্থায়ীভাবে আমেরিকায় বসবাস করেন । এই মামলা রমজু করার সময় পি, ডবি-উ-১ এর কোন আলোচনা হয় নাই। পরবর্তীতে আলোচনা হইয়াছে। তাই মামলাটি মজহরের ইংগিতে দায়ের হইয়াছে এই কথা প্রমান বহন করে। তবে পরবর্তীতে মজহরের সম্পত্তি থাকিতে পারে । যাহা হউক, যেহেতু মজহর নালিশী জমিতে শরীক নহেন এবং যেহেতু এই আইনের বিধানে পার্শ্ববর্তী জমির মালিক হিসাবে অগ্রক্রয়ের আবেদন করার সুযোগ নাই সেহেতু বিরোধীয় জমি প্রয়োজন এর বিষয়টি মুখ্য নহে। এখানে মুখ্য বিষয় হইতেছে নালিশী জমিতে শরীকের প্রশ্নটি কাজেই এই মামলার মজহর কোন প্রতিকার পাইতে অধিকারী নহেন।”

19. Having considered all those facts, the circumstances and the evidence on record, we find that there is no substance in the argument advanced by the learned Advocate appearing on behalf of the pre-emptor-appellant. 

20. In the light of the facts and circumstances discussed above, we do not find any illegality or infirmity in the impugned judgment, which in our view does not call for any interference. 

21. Accordingly, the appeal is dismissed without any order as to costs. 

End.

full_judgment:
Md Nuruzzaman, J: This Civil Appeal, by leave, has arisen out of the judgment and order dated 24-11-2004 passed by the High Court Division in Writ Petition No.3094 of 2000 making the Rule Nisi absolute with direction. 

2. Facts, leading to filing of this civil appeal, in short, are that: One Mussammat Masuda Khanam, daughter of Manik Lal Din acquired land measuring 1,000 square yards being Plot No.22/5 of Block-B of Plan No.132/i of 61/62 dated 27-7-1961 by virtue of a permanent registered lease deed being No.4853 dated 21-7-1962. Thereafter, said Masuda Khanam constructed two-storied pucca building thereon and resided therewith her family. Since Masuda Khanam was in need of cash money, she mortgaged the said two-storied building by obtaining a loan of Taka 50,000 on 19-2-1971 from the writ-petitioner on condition to repay the same within 15 years with interest at the rate of 10% per annum. It was stipulated in the mortgage deed that if Masuda Khanam failed to repay the said loan in time the writ-petitioner as respondent herein had the right to foreclose the said mortgage property. In view of the stipulation in the mortgage deed the writ petitioner took possession of the said house property at the time of execution of the mortgage deed. Since, then the writ petitioner along with his family members were residing in the said house. Thereafter, the writ petitioner was forcibly dispossessed by some miscreants from the said house in March 1971. After the liberation of Bangladesh, the writ petitioner went to the said house and found some relatives of Masuda Khanam then residing the said house on her behalf. The writ petitioner then approached to Mussammat Masuda Khanam who was then residing at a different address and location in Dhaka and found Masuda Khanam ill. The writ-petitioner asked Masuda Khanam either to refund the money of loan or to give him back the mortgage property after vacating her relatives therefrom. Then Masuda Khanam requested the writ-petitioner to allow her some time. The writ-petitioner having found Masuda seriously ill conceded to her request. In this way, some years passed by but Masuda Khanam failed to restore possession of the mortgage house to the writ-petitioner till February, 1986. The writ-petitioner was then compelled to file Title Suit No.438 of 1988 on 31-12-1988 against said Masuda Khanam and the Ministry of Housing and Works, Government of Bangladesh for foreclosure of the mortgage. The said mortgage suit was decreed ex-parte on 12-11-1990 and accordingly, Title Execution. Case No.15 of 1991 was filed. Subsequently, the Court's bailiff with the warrant of possession obtained from the executing Court went to the said property to hand over possession of the said house but found out that a tenant inducted by the writ-respondent No.1 was in possession of the said property. Accordingly, delivery of possession could not be handed over to the writ-petitioner. Thus, a report to that effect was submitted on 12-9-1991. The writ petitioner then came to know for the first time that the said house property was enlisted in the. "Ka" list as abandoned property. He filed the case before the Court of Settlement for release of the said house property by excluding the same from the "Ka" list. But the Court of Settlement refused to entertain the said settlement case on the ground that it was time barred. Therefore, in these backgrounds of the case, the writ petitioner served legal notice upon the writ respondents demanding justice but in vain. The writ petitioner finding no other alternative efficacious remedy moved the above mentioned writ petition before the High Court. Division and obtained the Rule Nisi. 

3. The writ-respondent No.1 contested the Rule Nisi by filing an affidavit-in-opposition asserting that the original allottee Masuda Khanam left Bangladesh just after liberation leaving the said house uncared for and the Government took it over as an abandoned property. 

4. A Division Bench of the High Court Division upon hearing the parties made the Rule Nisi absolute, with a direction to the writ respondents to exclude the House No.22/5, Block-B, Mohammadpur, Dhaka from the "Ka" list of Abandoned Building published by the Government dated 23-9-1986 at serial No.65 of page No.9762(16) forthwith. The writ respondents are also directed to restore the vacant possession of the said house to the writ petitioner within 3(three) months from the date of receipt of this order by the impugned judgment and order dated 24-11-2004. 

5. The Government of Bangladesh and another, feeling aggrieved by the impugned judgment and order dated 24-11-2004 of the High Court Division preferred the Civil Petition for Leave to Appeal No.1759 of 2009 before this Division and obtained leave, which, gave rise to the instant appeal.

6. Mr AM Amin Uddin, the learned Attorney-General appearing on behalf of the appellants submits that the High Court Division upon surmises and conjectures made the Rule Nisi absolute giving direction to hand over the possession of the property to the writ petitioner overlooking the provision that the list published under sub-section (1) of section 5 of the Ordinance No.LIV of 1985 shall 'be conclusive evidence of the fact that the buildings included therein are abandoned property and have been vested in the Government. He further submits that the respondent as per provision of section 7 of Ordinance No.LIV of 1985 did not apply for release within statutory period and, as such, the Court of Settlement rejected the application as barred by limitation, and, the High Court Division upon non-consideration of the facts about limitation made the Rule Nisi absolute with direction. He finally submits that from the record it is found that the respondent No.1 made averment that he obtained decree in a suit for foreclosure of the mortgaged property on "12-11-1990 being Title Suit No.438 of 1988, the High Court Division perused the decree dated 9-10-1990 and directed to release the property from "Ka" list in holding that the writ petitioner acquired ownership in that house by the said decree in the foreclosure suit which is a non-consideration of real fact but the High Court Division committed serious illegality in making the Rule Nisi absolute with direction, and, as such, the impugned judgment and order passed by the High Court Division is liable to be set-aside. Hence, the instant appeal may kindly be allowed.

7. Per contra, Mr Nurul Islam Bhuiyan, the learned Advocate-on-Record appearing on behalf of the respondent submits that the original owner of the said house, Masuda Khanam was all along present in the country, even after, the said house was mortgaged to the writ petitioner and the possession, thereof, was handed over to him in February, 1971. The writ petitioner was forcibly dispossessed from the possession by the miscreants in March, 1971. The writ petitioner during abnormal period, during the liberation war resided at some other place with his family members and could not take any step for recovery of possession of the said house. After the war of liberation, he found out that some relatives of the original owner, Masuda Khanam was in occupation of the said property. Thereafter, he contacted Masuda Khanam and asked her to restore the vacant possession of the house to him when Masuda Khanam in view of her precarious health condition at the relevant time requested the writ petitioner to wait for some time to which the writ petitioner agreed. Thereafter, the writ petitioner having found that Masuda Khanam was unduly delaying to hand over possession Of the said house, and, hence, he filed suit for foreclosure of the mortgage property and obtained decree on 12-11-90. Till that time, the Government did not take over possession of the said house as an abandoned property and subsequently, without forming any opinion whether the said house was liable to be treated as an abandoned property or not took over possession of the same without taking any step or issuing any notice on the occupant of the house under Article 7 of the Bangladesh Abandoned Property (Control, Management and Disposal) Order, 1972 (PO 16 of 1972) by inducting tenant and also included the same in the "Ka" list as an abandoned building. Although the Government was a party as defendant to the said title suit for foreclosure, the Government did not contest the suit resisting the claim of the writ petitioner that it was an abandoned property. The writ petitioner has filed original documents including the registered lease deed and also the mortgage deed showing that the said house originally belonged to Masuda Khanam and subsequently, the writ petitioner acquired the same on the basis of a decree in a mortgage suit for foreclosure and, as such, the High Court Division rightly passed the impugned judgment. Therefore, on above backdrops the impugned judgment calls for no interference by this Division. Hence, the instant appeal may kindly be dismissed. 

8. We have heard the learned Attorney-General for the appellants and the learned Advocate-on-record for the respondent. Perused the impugned judgment of the High Court Division and other connected materials on record. 

9. The moot questions before this Division is whether High Court Division has failed to appreciate the relevant provisions of law of Abandoned Property in its true prospective in the present case and thereby committed serious error of law in making the rule absolute. 

10. The writ petitioner respondents claimed that he got the property through registered mortgage deed from one Masuda Khanam who obtained permanent lease vide lease deed No.4855 dated 21-7-1962. The writ petitioner was in possession of the Property. In the March, 1971 he dispossessed by some miscreants forcibly. After Liberation the petitioner approached the Masuda Khanam to refund the money or to restore the Possession of the property as her relatives were in Possession. Masuda Khatun requested him to give some time as she was ill. Ultimately, Masuda Khanam did not take any steps and in this way some years had been passed. The writ Petitioner as mortgagee filed title suit in the year 1988 for foreclosure and the suit was decreed ex-parte as none contested in the suit. He filed the title execution and got order of possession. However, the court's Bailiff could not handover the possession as he found the tenant of the writ respondent No.1 was in the Possession of the suit property. After getting such information the writ petitioner filed a case before the Court of Settlement for release of the property. The Court of Settlement refused to entertain the case as it was time barred. In these backdrops, the writ petitioner filed the instant writ petition before the High Court Division. 

11. The High Court Division in the Judgment simply opined that the Government was party in the suit for foreclosure but did not raise any objection stating that the suit Property is abandoned Property. Further found that the writ Petitioner had all original documents from the Masuda Khanom, the owner of the Property. The High Court Division also found that the concerned authority without forming any opinion whether the house in question was liable to be treated as an abandoned property or not, and took over the Possession without serving any notice on the occupant of the house. The High Court Division also found that by dint of ex-parte decree in the foreclosure suit got the title over the suit Property. Hence, made the Rule absolute. 

12. It reveals that the property was listed as abandoned on 28-2-1972 when PO No.16 of 1972 came into force as the real owner Masuda Khanam being totally absent and his whereabouts were untraceable. Thereafter, on 23-9-1986 while gazette notification was published under section 5(1) of the Ordinance No.54 of 1985 enlisting the property in "Ka" list as an abandoned Property. The writ Petitioner filed the foreclosure suit on 31-12-1988 being Title Suit No.438 of 1988 and obtained ex-parte decree on 12-11-1990 much later of the enlistment of the Property as an abandoned Property under section 5(1) of the Ordinance No.54 of 1985. Moreover, according to Article 2(1) of the Bangladesh Abandoned Property (Control, Management and Disposal) Order 1972 (PO 16 of 1972) the property was declared as abandoned property, the provision of Article 2(1) is quoted below: "'Abandoned Property' means any property owned by any person who is not present in Bangladesh or whose whereabouts are not known or who has ceased to occupy, supervise or manage in person his property, including—
(i) any property owned by any person who is a citizen of a State which at any time after the 25th day of March, 1971, was at war with or engaged in military operations against the People's Republic of Bangladesh; 
(ii) Any property taken over under the Bangladesh (Taking Over of Control and Management of Industrial and Commercial Concerns) Order, 1972 (Acting President's Order No.1 of 1972), but does not include—
(a)	any property the owner of which is residing outside Bangladesh for any purpose which, in the opinion of the Government, is not prejudicial to the interest of Bangladesh; 
(b)	any property which is in the possession or under the control of the Government under any law for the time being in force. 
Explanation:—"Person who is not present in Bangladesh" includes anybody of persons or company constituted or incorporated in the territory or under the laws of a State which at any time after the 25th day of March, 1971, was at war with or engaged in military operations against the Peoples' Republic of Bangladesh: 
[(la) "authorized officer" means an officer authorized by the Government for the purpose of this Order"]" 

13. It further reveals from the Provisions of section 5(2) of the Ordinance No.54 of 1985 that such enlistment shall be conclusive evidence thus, the Provisions of the section 5(2) is quoted below: 
"5(2).—The lists published under sub-section (1) shall be conclusive evidence of the fact that the buildings included therein are abandoned property and have vested in the Government as such." 

14. In the facts of the present case it appears that the Masuda Khanom has ever appeared in any court proceedings or claiming the Property by filing any application to the concerned authority praying for releasing of the Property from abandoned list. The writ petitioner in his writ application first averred the he had been dispossessed by some miscreants, however, soon after the independence he found the relative of the Masuda Khanom had been living in the Property. He without trying to take Possession approached the Masuda, this story create serious doubt about his possession before independence because if he was in possession why did not take any steps against the miscreants. Moreso, it was found by the Court's bailiff that the Government allottee is in possession in the Property. This proved that possession of the writ petitioner in the Property was a story creating for the purpose of the case by the power of Attorney of the writ petitioner as the case was not filed by the writ Petitioner but his attorney. 

15. This Division has held in the case of Gannysons Ltd. vs Sonali Bank reported in 36 DLR (AD) 146, that once a Property vests in the Government under Presidents Order No.16 of 1972 no legal proceedings can be taken against such property. 

16. This view we find support from the Provisions of Article 14 of the PO No.16 of 1972 thus runs as follows: 
Exception from legal process 
"14.(1)Any property vested in the Government under this Order shall be exempt from all legal process, including seizure, distress, ejectment, attachment or sale by any officer of a Court or any other authority, and no injunction or other order of whatever kind in respect of such property shall be granted or made by any Court or any other authority, and the Government shall not be divested or dispossessed of such property by operation of any law for the time being in force.
(2) Any , such legal process as aforesaid subsisting immediately before the commencement of this Order shall cease to have effect on such commencement and all abandoned properties in custody of any Court, receiver, guardian or other person or persons appointed by it, shall upon delivery of the same being called for by the Government, be delivered to the Government. 
(3) No Court shall pass an order in any suit or proceeding granting a temporary or ad-interim injunction restraining the Government or the Deputy Commissioner or the Sub-divisional Magistrate or the authorized officer, or any other officer or person acting under the authority, orders or directions of any of them, from taking possession of any property if any notice under, or purported to be under, any provision of this Order has been served 'upon any person requiring or directing him to surrender possession of such property, and, any such order passed by any Court before the commencement of the Bangladesh Abandoned Property (Control, Management and Disposal) (Amendment) Ordinance, 1976 (LV of 1976), shall stand vacated and cease to have effect". 

17. In the case of Rahima Begum vs Court of Settlement reported in 2 BLC (AD) 108 it has held that—
"If the building in question carries a presumption of being abandoned property it is exempt from any legal process, be it an auction sale by the Government itself or through, Court. The petitioners carried the onus to prove the presence or whereabouts or management of the building in question by the original non-Bengali owner when President's Order No.16 of 1972 was promulgated and this burden of proof having not been discharged by them before the Court of Settlement, no case for releasing the holding in question from the list of abandoned property has been made out." 

18. In the present case the real owner was totally absent from the legal proceedings instituted against her. Moreso, she had not made any representation to the Government for restoration the possession of her property or praying from releasing the property from abandoned list as she was not in possession of the property. Thus, the onus was shifted upon the claimant not on the Government to prove that the owner was present in Bangladesh, she has occupy, supervisor or manage in person her Property. 

19. The question of serving notice upon her as opined by the High Court Division in the facts and circumstances as discussed hereinabove is nothing but nugatory. The High Court Division relied to the case of Bangladesh vs Amela Khatun, reported in 53 DLR (AD) 55, the facts of the relied case is totally distinguishable from the facts of the instant case. In the referred case, there was no legal Proceedings, neither the owner of the case property was not untraceable nor non-Bengali, thus, that decision cannot squarely applicable in the present case. 

20. It is perhaps pertinent in the instant case to address the question as to whether the ex-parte decree in a case of foreclosure in respect of enlisted abandoned property would be binding effect against the Government as the High Court Division held in the instant case. 

21. In a mortgage the stipulations are to be settled between the mortgagor and mortgagee, the Government has no function in the private mortgage deed, so, the issue to be decided in a such suit for foreclosure between the mortgagor and mortgagee, whether, mortgage is genuine, and stipulations of the mortgage was proved or not, so, even if, in the suit the Government is defendant nothing has to be decided against the Government, in the suit for foreclosure, such a decree in law is not binding upon the Government for the enlisted abandoned property. However, the High Court Division has missed the point as discussed hereinabove. Therefore, by dint of ex-parte decree in the instant foreclosure suit the writ petitioner did not acquire any right and title in the case property. 

22. In the case of Government of the People's Republic of Bangladesh vs M/s Speedbird Navigation Co. reported in 30 DLR (SC) 101 this Division has held that, "No doubt the determination is only an ascertainment of fact constituting a property an abandoned property, and on such preliminary ascertainment of fact the law takes effect of its own force from 28-2-72 the date the Order came into force. On such formation of opinion of the Government after ascertainment of the fact the property as abandoned property." 

23. In the instant case the Bailiff of the Court found that the allottee of respondent No.1 is in possession of the house in question. So, while writ respondent allotted the suit property to allottee, the Government has already formed an opinion that the suit property was an abandoned property. 

24. Having given our most anxious consideration to the discussions made hereinabove and authorities cited, we cannot but to held that the High Court Division has surely missed the yardstick to determine that the writ petitioner by dint of an ex-parte decree in a suit for foreclosure did not acquire any right and title in the case property. 

Accordingly, this appeal is allowed. The judgment of the High Court Division is hereby set-aside. However, without any order as to costs. 

End.

full_judgment:
Let a Rule be issued calling upon the opposite parties to show cause as to why the impugned judgment and order dated 9-8-2017 passed by the learned Senior District Judge, Jashore in Pratarpon Appeal No. 28 of 2016 dismissing the appeal and thereby affirming the judgment and order dated 10-8-2016 passed by the Joint District Judge, 1st Court and Arpita Shampatti Prottarpon Tribunal, Jashore in vested Property Case No. 1161 of 2014 should not be set-aside and/or pass such other or further order or orders as to this Court may seem fit and proper. 

2. Facts in short are that the opposite party No. 1 as plaintiff filed above vested case No. 1161 of 2014 in the court of Arpito Shampatti Prottarpan Tribunal for release of scheduled property alleging that the disputed property belonged to Suraj Bashini who had no child. So she adopted Niva Rani Dhar and Ganga Narayan Chakraverty and made a will in favour of them on 31-1-1965. Above Niva Rani and Ganga Narayan got probate on 21-5-1966 in probate case No 15 of 1965. The Government filed revocation case No. 157 of 1969 which was dismissed on 14-11-1972. Niva Rani filed an Eviction case being No. 409 of 1967 for disputed property which was decreed and an appeal filed against above judgment and decree was dismissed. A second appeal to the High Court Division was also dismissed. Opposite Party No. 1 purchased the scheduled property from above Niva Rani Dhar by a registered kobla deed on 29-10-1979. 

3. Opposite party Nos. 2-3 the Government of Bangladesh represented by Deputy Commissioner contested the case by filling a written statement. It was alleged that the disputed property belonged to Suraj Bashini who left this Country for good for India in 1965 and the suit property was enlisted as vested property and all the documents of the plaintiff are forged, collusive and not acted upon. 

4. In the above suit petitioner filed a petition under order 1 rule 10 of the Code of Civil procedure for being added as a defendant. It was alleged that the scheduled property was owned and held by Suraj Bashini who left this country for good for India in 1965 and the suit property was enlisted as vested property. This petitioner is possessing the suit property for about 60 years on getting lease from the government. 

5. On consideration of submissions made by the learned Advocates for both sides and materials on record the learned Joint District Judge rejected the petition holding that since the petitioner is a lessee of the Government he has no right distinct and separate from the Government who is contesting the case. 

6. Being aggrieved by above judgment and order the petitioner preferred Appeal No. 28 of 2016 to the District Judge, Jessore who on consideration of submissions of learned the advocates for both sides and materials on record dismissed the appeal and affirmed the order of the trial Court. 

7. Being aggrieved by above judgment and order of the District Judge the petitioner has moved this Court and obtained this rule. 

8. Mr Md Abul Kalam Azad, learned Advocate for the petitioner submits that the petitioner is in possession of the scheduled property for more than 60 years and has acquired a valuable right which can be better protected by this petitioner himself if he is allowed to be added as a defendant in the case. If the petitioner is impleaded as a defendant that will not in any way cause any inconvenience or loss to the plaintiff. But his addition in the case will provide valuable support and will be helpful to the Government and to the Court to arrive at a correct decision in the case. In order to avoid multiplicity of suits the learned District Judge should have allowed the petition under order 1 rule 10 of the Code of Civil Procedure. But the learned District Judge rejected the petition on erroneous view of both facts and laws which is not tenable in law. In support of his submission the learned Advocate has referred to the case law reported in 49 DLR at page-117. 

9. On the other hand, Mr Md Ekramul Islam, learned Advocate for the opposite party no. 1 submits that the Arpito Shampotti Prottarpan Ain 2001 (hereinafter referred to as Ain) is a special law. Section 3 of the above Ain contains an overriding clause over other laws and section 4 restricts the applicability of the Code of Civil Procedure in any proceedings under the Ain. The Code of Civil Procedure will be applicable only as far as the same is provided under the Ain and section 11 of the Code of Civil Procedure. The provision of Order 1 Rule 10 of the Code of Civil Procedure has not been made application in any proceedings under the AM. Since the Government is contesting the case and as a lessee of the Government the petitioner has no separate right or claim he is not a necessary party. As such the learned Courts below rightly found that the petitioner is not a necessary party in the proceedings under the Ain and rejected his petition which calls for no interference. 

10. Considered the submissions of the Learned Advocates of respective parties and perused the impugned order and other materials on record. 

11. At the very outset it needs to be mentioned that the petitioner in his petition under Order I Rule 10 of the Code of Civil Procedure claimed to be a lessee of the scheduled property under the Government. 

12. But in his application before this Court under section 115(4) of the Code of Civil Procedure the Petitioner has made a different claim. He did not mention that he is a lessee under the Government. At paragraph 8 of the revisional application the petitioner has claimed title and possession in the Scheduled property on the basis of payment of Taka 35,000 to one Shreedhar Kumar Das. 

13. But the learned Advocate for the petitioner did not make any mention of above claim of title of the petitioner at the time of hearing. The learned Advocate submitted that the petitioner is in possession of the scheduled property for more than 60 years as a lessee under the Government. 

14. The Aripto Sampatti Prottorpon Ain, 2001 (hereinafter referred to as Ain) is a special law section 3 of the Ain clearly mentions that the provisions of the Ain shall prevail notwith-standing anything contained in any other law for the time being in force. Section 4 of the Ain provides for restricted application of the Code of Civil Procedure in any proceedings under the Ain. It provides that section 11 of the Code of Civil Procedure will be applicable and other provisions of the Code will be applicable subject to the provisions of this Ain. No provision of the Ain provides for addition of parties in any proceedings under the AM. Nor the provision of Order 1 Rule 10 of the Code of Civil Procedure has been made applicable in any proceedings under the Ain. 

15. Section 10 of the Ain provides the procedure for receipt of cases or applications and disposal of those by the Arpito Shampatti Prortopon Tribunal. Subsection 6(kha) of above section provides that if the Tribunal accepts any petition for adjudication then it shall issue a notice of the same upon the concerned Deputy Commissioner. Subsection 8(ka) provides that the Tribunal shall hear the petitioner in support of its claim and the reply of the Government represented by the Deputy Commissioner, if any, before making a decision in the case. 

16. Above provisions clearly show that in any proceedings under the Ain only the Government represented by the Deputy Commissioner is a necessary party. The Deputy Commissioner who will have to be notified and heard by the Tribunal in any proceedings before it. The Ain does not make any provision for the Tribunal to notify or hear any third person other than the petitioner and the Government. 

17. Above provisions reflect true intention behind the promulgation of the Ain. The objective of the Ain is to return the vested properties to its original owners or their legal successors who are citizens of Bangladesh. Since the Government by promulgation of law took up the possession and management of the vested properties only Government will be heard by the Tribunal to determine the petition of the claimants. 

18. Moreover, as a mere lessee the petitioner does not have any claim or right which is distinct and separate from that of the Government who is already a defendant in the proceedings. The facts and laws of the case referred to above by the learned Advocate for the petitioner is distinguish-able from those of the case in hand. As such above case law has no manner of applicable in this case. 

19. On consideration of above materials, I am of the view that in any proceedings under the Ain only the Government represented by the Deputy Commissioner is a necessary party and a lessee of the Government or any other person is not a necessary party to be impleaded ad defendant in above proceedings and the provision of Order 1 Rule 10 of the Code of Civil Procedure is not applicable in any proceeding under the Ain. 

20. The learned District Judge on correct appreciation of relevant laws and materials on record has rightly dismissed the appeal and affirmed the order of the trial Court which calls for no interference. 

21. This Court finds no merit in the instant Civil Revision case and this rule deserves to be discharged. 

22. In the result, this rule is discharged without any order as to costs. 

23. The ad-interim order passed at the time of issuance of the rule is hereby vacated. 

Let the lower Court's record along with a copy of this judgment be transmitted down to the Court concerned at once. 

End.
