parties:
Naina Islam ------- Petitioner
Vs.
Bangladesh and others ------- Respondents
full_judgment:
Syed Refaat Ahmed, J: This Rule Nisi was issued on 2-5-2011 calling upon the Respondents to show cause as to why they should not be directed to evict the trespassers from the case land measuring 5 (five) kathas of Plot No. 10 (ten), Road No. 1/A of Gulshan Residential Area, Police Station-Gulshan, Dhaka ("said property") and hand-over the vacant possession of the same to the petitioner in accordance with law and/or such other or further order or orders passed as to this Court may seem fit and proper.
2. The petitioner filed this Writ Petition for enforcement of her right to property guaranteed under Article 42 of the Constitution and to enjoy the protection of law and to be treated only in accordance with law as under article 31 of the Constitution.
3. The said property was initially allotted to one Dr. M. Rafiquzzaman by the Respondent No. 2, Rajdhani Unnayan Katripakkhya represented by its Chairman ("RAJUK"). RAJUK registered the Deed of Transfer, i.e., Lease Deed No. 13645 in favour of Dr. M. Rafiquzzaman on 28-12-1989 for a period of ninety-nine years. It so transpired that the petitioner, Mrs. Naina Islam having shown interest to purchase the said property from Mr M. Rafiquzzaman the latter applied to RAJUK on 1-3-1998 for a sale permission as was accorded on 3-11-1999. Consequentially, the petitioner purchased the said property through a registered sale Deed No. 16033 of 15-11-1999.
4. Thereafter, upon the petitioner's application; her name was mutated in place of the vendor Mr M. Rafiquzzaman in RAJUK's record vide Memo No. RAJUK/Estate/33/2 dated 4-1-2000.
5. Against this general backdrop, it is contended, at the dead of night on 17-12-2008, the petitioner's resident caretaker (who looks after the property on behalf of the petitioner and her husband who reside abroad) was evicted from the said property by trespassers causing the petitioner to, thereby, lose possession of her property. This caused the petitioner to lodge a General Diary against the trespassers being GD No. 2161 of 25-12-2008.
6. The petitioner took further strident steps for recovering possession of her property and in that regard petitioned the Respondent No. 3, Chairman, RAJUK (received apparently through the State Minister, Ministry of Housing and Public Works who forwarded the petition initially to the Respondent No. 5, Secretary, RAJUK on 15-4-2009) for immediate eviction of the trespassers. She prayed consequentially for a restoration of her possession. It so transpired that RAJUK initiated an eviction process scheduled for 31-12-2009 by requesting the Commissioner, Dhaka Metropolitan Police to engage his force to maintain law and order in aid of such eviction exercise. Predicated on these developments, it is contended, the Respondent No. 5 arranged for two platoons of police force for eviction of the trespassers from the said property. Accordingly, the Respondent No. 7, Magistrate, RAJUK is to have initially embarked on an eviction exercise on 31-12-2009 but inexplicably abandoned that exercise and retreated from the said property without actually evicting the trespassers. It is submitted that the petitioner, therefore, remains wholly in the dark till today about such volte face by the said Respondents.
7. This is all the more surprising given that pursuant to the petitioner's Application of 15-4-2009. RAJUK on 29-6-2009 decided to hold an inquiry as to the petitioner's dispossession from the said property on 6-7-2009. The inquiry report produced recorded the fact that the said property was locked up with no one residing there and that in that case necessary steps could be taken to launch an eviction drive.
8. The petitioner states that RAJUK decided to seek advice from its legal adviser on 5.8.2009 who reverted on 19-8-2009 with the advice that necessary assistance could be provided to the petitioner to evict the trespassers from the said property.
9. There is yet another dimension to this case that needs to be recorded here. The petitioner's case plays out against the backdrop of previous dealings in the said property that have come to bear upon her possessory and occupancy rights therein. This history of the claims and counter claims to the said property was only brought on record by the petitioner on 31.7.2016 through the second Supplementary Affidavit filed on her behalf.
10. The first date of note is 26-7-1964 when 32.85 acres of land of Mouza Bhola, PS Tejgaon, Dhaka (then Dacca) was ordered to be acquired by the then Additional Deputy Commissioner, Dacca in LA Case No. 10763-64 for extension of Gulshan Model Town. It is on 23-12-1964 that 31.34 acres land in the said Mouza including CS Plot No. 457 owned by one Mr Abdur Rahim was similarly ordered to be acquired with immediate effect, also under LA Case No. 10/63-64. Thirteen years later an order was passed on 31-3-1977 by the Joint Secretary of Ministry of Works regarding derequisition of 32.85 acres of land in LA Case No. 10/63-64. However, on 10-9-1977 a Final Requisition Order was passed by the Joint Secretary of Ministry of Works reviewing the Order dated 31-3-1977 regarding derequisition of 32.85 acres of land in LA Case No. 10/63-64. Being aggrieved by such Final Requisition Order one Mr Khademul Islam filed Writ Petition No. 835 of 1977 in respect of the scheme of acquisition of 32.85 acres of land in LA Case No. 10/63-64. The Rule was made absolute in Writ Petition No. 835 of 1977 on 12-7-1979, thereby, effectively upholding the order of derequisition of 31-3-1977.
11. It is noted that this state of affairs continued for twenty-eight years until the derequisition process itself was found to be illegal, as we shall see by the High Court Division on 15-11-2007. By doing so the High Court Division in effect restored in 2007 the status quo ante granting validity to the acquisition process as commenced earlier in 1964.
12. From RAJUK's pleadings in this case it is evident that its account begins here as the initial requiring body. Having in that capacity devised the RAJUK Layout Plan, it allotted to Dr. M Rafiquzzaman the said property on 5-12-1989 which allotment can be termed as a direct consequence of the 1964 acquisition process.
13. It is in this factual milieu that both Dr. M. Rafiquzzaman and the petitioner Mrs. Naina Islam appear on the scene between 1989 and 1998 as already above recorded.
14. A development of note as brought forth in the petitioner's second Supplementary Affidavit of 31-7-2016 occurred at this juncture. That is, on 8-2-1999 the Ministry of Land issued a notice directing the District Commissioner, Dhaka to take necessary steps to cancel the proceedings of LA Case No. 10/63-64 pursuant to the judgment dated 12-7-1979 in Writ Petition No. 835 of 1977. While parallel to these developments by the end of 1999 the petitioner, Mrs Naina Islam had already acquired a firm and entrenched title to the said property as above noted through a deed registered in her favour.
15. Pursuant to the Land Ministry's Order of 8-2-1999 a gazette of derequisitioned properties, including that of Mr Abdur Rahim, having been published on 11-11-1999 there was another development of note evident in a Review Petition being No. 13 of 1999 arising out of Writ Petition No. 835 of 1977 being rejected on 22-11-1999 by the Court. Drawing on parallel timelines related to this case, it is noted that soon after the said property was mutated in the petitioner's name in Mutation Case No. 111 of 2000 on 27-1-2000 the Appellate Division at the other hand dismissed on 31-7-2001 the Civil Petition for Leave to Appeal being 122 of 2000 arising out of Review Petition No. 13 of 1999 and Writ Petition No. 835 of 1977. Accordingly, this gave rise to the situation where on the one hand the petitioner Mrs. Naina Islam was paying taxes and rates on the said property from 2000 to 2016, conflicting and potentially rival rights and interests were being created concerning the said property by forces unleashed through the judgment in Writ Petition No. 835 of 1977.
16. It is to be noted, however, that while pursuant to the outcome of CPLA No. 122 of 2000 a gazette notification was published on 2.8.2001 concerning the derequisition of 14.6842 acres of land from RAJUK the plot of Mr Abdur Rahim was not included in that list. Notably, RAJUK also filed Writ Petition No. 5198 of 2003 against the said gazette notification of 2-8-2001 as to the derequisitioned 14.6842 acres of land.
17. It is against this backdrop that Mr Abdur Rahim executed "saf kabala" in favour of the Added Respondent No. 8, Mr Abdus Salam Mazumder, termed by the petitioner to be the trespasser in this case, in relation to the sale of 16 and 2 Katha of land on 25-10-2004 and 1-11-2004 respectively. In the following period Mr Abdus Salam Mazumder applied for electricity and gas connections from the relevant utility service providers but having failed to acquire a clearance certificate from RAJUK filed Writ Petition No. 8679 of 2005. The High Court Division on 4-12-2005 having directed RAJUK to dispose of Mr Mazumder's application for a Clearance Certificate, the said Clearance Certificate was eventually issued by RAJUK on 2-10-2007.
18. In the meantime a judgment of the High Court Division on 15-11-2007 in Writ Petition Nos. 5198 of 2003, 11817 of 2006, 11818 of 2006, 11819 of 2006 and 3466 of 2007 declared the gazette notifications as to derequisitions to be illegal.
19. Consequentially, Mr Abdur Rahim finally exited from the scene and the petitioner's predecessor Dr. M. Rafiquzzaman stepped in. The petitioner asserts that it is in this context that the rights and interests of Mr Abdur Rahim finally got extinguished and that of the petitioner's predecessor Dr. M. Rafiquzzaman revived. Through the judgment of 15-11-2007 the status quo ante was, accordingly, restored vis-a-vis the 1964 acquisition process.
20. The petitioner is all the more baffled at the sudden abandonment of the eviction process given that she had deposited Taka 70,000 for that very purpose at RAJUK's request. This set of facts provides the immediate backdrop for filing the instant Writ petitioner.
21. It is pertinent to note at the outset that RAJUK has appeared in this case acknowledging the petitioner to be its actual lessee and also admitting that it has acted on the petitioner's application by taking steps to evict Mr Abdus Salam Mazumder, the trespasser, who has been added as the added Respondent No. 8 by virtue of this Court's Order dated 16-7-2017. A copy of that Order being duly served upon him as per our later Order of 21-11-2017, Mr Mazumder has not contested the Rule. For its part, despite the acknowledgment and admission as noted above, RAJUK claims nevertheless that this Writ Petition is not maintainable.
22. With RAJUK's unexplained volte face about evicting Mr Mazumder in mind, the petitioner, Mrs. Naina Islam puts forward the central thesis of her case. She asserts that given that RAJUK is the allotter of the said property under whose supervision the petitioner enjoys the rights of the ultimate lease holder, RAJUK by that reason is under an obligation to protect her right to property guaranteed under article 42 of the Constitution. By extension, according to the petitioner, RAJUK is also under a duty to recover the property of the petitioner, restore possession to her and, thereby, secure to her the protection of the law as enshrined in article 31 of the Constitution.
23. The Respondent Nos. 2 and 3 being RAJUK and its Chairman respectively are represented in these proceedings by their learned Advocate, Mr Md Imam Hasan. By filing an Affidavit-in-Opposition the said Respondents preliminarily assert that this Writ Petition is not maintainable. This stance predicated on their understanding that they have been divested of all responsibility regarding overseeing and protecting possessory and occupancy rights regarding the said property as early as on 23-12-1989 when the said plot was handed over to the original allottee, Dr. M. Rafiquzzaman. It is specifically submitted in that light that it remains the sole duty of the occupant-lessee in possession of the said property, i.e., someone in the position of the petitioner, Mrs Naina Islam to herself secure all rights incidental upon such possession and that in any case a matter of dispossession as this is to be agitated in a proper legal forum other one of judicial review as this. The Respondents have, however, not taken care to specify what other forum(s) may indeed be available to the petitioner in the circumstances. Having said that, the Affidavit-in-Opposition nevertheless reads to this Court as an attestation of all facts asserted by the petitioner as to her chain of title to the said property and the acquisition of such title through a permission of transfer from the original allottee granted by RAJUK itself. In other words, this Court notes at the outset, RAJUK asserts the petitioner's sole and exclusive right to control the said property and to exclude others therefrom.
24. It is in the above context that RAJUK also acknowledges that upon the petitioner's prayer RAJUK by a letter dated 20-10-2009 asked the trespassers to vacate the said property. However, there is evident a note of equivocation on part of the Respondents at this stage in presenting their version of the facts. Beyond the acknowledgement of issuance of the said letter of 20-10-2009 the Affidavit-in-Opposition does not specifically attest further the fact of RAJUK having actually initiated the eviction process on 24-12-2009 by requesting the Commissioner, Dhaka Metropolitan Police to deploy two platoons of police force in the interest of law and order while the eviction exercise of 31-12-2009 would be underway (Annexure 'E'). There is no specific denial by the Respondents either as to the actual issuance of such Annexure 'E' document or indeed the authenticity of the same.
25. It is to be noted here that the Affidavit-in-Opposition is wholly silent on the history of the said property involving LA Case No. 10/63-64 and its aftermath as has been extensively recorded above.
26. In presenting the petitioner's case, the learned Advocate Mr Ajmalul Hossain submits at the outset that despite several oral representations from the petitioner, RAJUK has persistently declined to disclose any reason for a sudden change of mind in evicting trespassers from the said property. Even after receiving a Notice Demanding Justice RAJUK is shown not to have taken any effective measures for eviction and handing over the vacant possession of the said property to the petitioner.
27. The petitioner being aggrieved by RAJUK's volte face and inertia, has resultantly filed the instant Writ Petition for enforcement of her fundamental rights as protected under Article 42 of the Constitution. In this context, Mr Ajmalul Hossain submits that the petitioner, being a lessee of RAJUK, has the right to be in possession of the said property without let or hindrance, but the added Respondent No. 8 interfered with such possession by virtue of a deed purportedly executed by the original owners and also by virtue of a purported clearance certificate ostensibly issued by RAJUK in respect of the said property.
28. Mr Ajmalul Hossain submits further that the petitioner's status and position to pursue her claim of recovery against RAJUK is further fortified by the fact that section 108(A)(b) of the Transfer of Property Act, 1882 clearly states that the lessor shall put the lessee into possession of the leased property at the lessee's request. Section 108(A)(c) also states that the lessor is under an obligation to ensure that the lessee possesses the leased property without interruption. By that reason, the petitioner's statutory right was infringed as RAJUK failed to fulfil its duty by ensuring peaceful possession of the petitioner in the said leased property. The petitioner having applied to RAJUK for eviction of the trespasser and RAJUK pursuant to such application having promised the petitioner to undertake the eviction process evident in requesting and accepting a deposit to defray the costs of such eviction backed off midway all on a sudden and lift the petitioner stranded and in a limbo without assigning any reasons despite several requests from the petitioner.
29. Mr Hossain submits that only the High Court Division can declare this inaction of RAJUK to be without lawful authority and of no legal effect as per article 102(2)(a)(ii) of the Constitution. Besides, it is only this Court that can issue an order in the manner of a writ in Mandamus directing RAJUK to evict the Respondent No. 8 from the said property and hand over the same to the petitioner, while exercising its special original jurisdiction under article 102(2)(a)(i) of the Constitution.
30. A yet more fundamental point is put forward by Mr Hossain. He argues that RAJUK is still the owner of the said property, whereas the petitioner is the lessee. The Respondent No. 8, Mr Mazumder who is alleged to have a registered deed in his favour from the original owner from whom the property was acquired for RAJUK, dispossessed the petitioner. The existence of the registered deed in favour of Mr Mazumder, according to Mr Hossain, does not bear relation to the legality of the lease in favour of the petitioner rather the same involves questions of RAJUK's title. Given that the said property was earlier acquired from Mr Mazumder's predecessor-in-interest, Mr Abdur Rahim, no residuary right vested in Mr Rahim after the acquisition process to transfer the said property to anyone. The acquisition process spelt an extinguishment of all of Mr Rahim's rights in the said property. Therefore, if at all, it is for RAJUK and not the petitioner to file a suit for declaration of its title over the said property.
31. It is at this juncture that the petitioner reiterates the speciousness of RAJUK's suggestion that she would be better off pursuing her claim if at all, in another forum. If, the petitioner submits, RAJUK is hinting at a suit for recovery of possession then that suggestion is without merit given that both section 108(A)(b) and (c) of the Transfer of Property Act, 1882 as submitted by Mr Ajmalul Hossain attach primarily to the lessor RAJUK's statutory responsibilities to secure the lessee petitioner's possessory and occupancy rights commensurate with the guarantees entrenched under Articles 42 and 31 of the Constitution. Therefore, it is for RAJUK now to ensure the petitioner's peaceful possession over the said leased property and since the petitioner was dispossessed from the same the petitioner's rightful recourse was to apply to RAJUK to get re-possession of the said property. That having yielded no positive outcome at the end of the day and instead being frustrated by RAJUK's inconsistent and opaque decisions the petitioner rightfully sought judicial review of such action and inaction.
32. If, on the other hand, the petitioner submits, the Respondents are hinting at the availability of alternate relief under, for example, the Specific Relief Act, 1877, then the remedy under section 9 of the Specific Relief Act is not an equally alternative efficacious remedy as the same confining itself to recovery of possession stops short of determining the title to such property and, thereby, does not prevent initiation of satellite litigation. Furthermore, RAJUK itself has led the petitioner to apply before it and has acted upon such application for evicting the trespassers, albeit partially, without at any material time ever expressing its inability to dispossess the Respondent No. 8 trespasser. In the meantime, of course, the period of limitation for filing a section 9 suit for recovery of possession has elapsed. Therefore, even if for the sake of argument it is considered that a suit for recovery of possession is the proper remedy for the petitioner, the same could not be instituted due to the actions of RAJUK and due to the impression created and promise given by RAJUK that it will take steps to evict the Respondent No. 8 from the said property and restore the petitioner's possession of the same.
33. Given the above circumstances it can be said that the remedy as set out in section 9 of the Specific Relief Act is not alternatively an equally efficacious remedy for the petitioner and, therefore, the Writ is maintainable. Whether the remedy available is equally efficacious or not is usually determined by the court by examining the facts and circumstances of each case. Relevantly, in Inland Navigation Co. vs Income Tax Officer reported in 19 DLR 87 (Para 16) the High Court Division entertained a writ petition even where the petitioner had an alternative option to file an appeal against the rectified order of assessment of income tax but failed to do so upon a misconception of the law. Therefore, even if the petitioner in this case was under a misconception of law in not filing a suit for recovery of possession, she should not be barred from pursuing this Writ Petition since such misconception was contributed by RAJUK by acting upon the petitioner's application and promising the petitioner to evict the trespasser.
34. Considering the above circumstances, this Court finds that this Writ Petition is indeed maintainable.
35. On the substantive issues raised, we find at the outset that the petitioner is the lawful lessee of RAJUK. Therefore, RAJUK finds itself in the position of a landlord of the leased property and is under an obligation to put the lessee into the possession of the leased property and to secure the quiet enjoyment of the lessee in the leased property. That relationship between the landlord and lessee would include the protection of the lessee from disturbance by strangers.
36. Section 108 of the Transfer of Property Act stipulates the rights and liabilities of the lessor and lessee as against one another in relation to any leased property. As per section 108(A)(b) "the lessor is bound on the lessee's request to put him in possession of the property." Further, as per section 108(A)(c) "the lessor shall be deemed to contract with the lessee that, if the latter pays the rent reserved by the lease and performs the contracts binding on the lessee, he may hold the property during the time limited by the lease without interruption." The legal regime protective of a lessee's rights to enjoyment of property without let or hindrance and as constitutes the rationale of the section 108 provisions above, is amply reflected in the following observation in Niazi Khanam vs Pakistan reported in PLD 1960 (WP) Karachi 616 (Page-622, Para B):
"The statutory rule under the common law is that the lessee is entitled to enjoy the properties leased out without interruption and there is an implied covenant that the lesser's title is such that no lawful entry, eviction or interruption will occur."
37. In the case of Ram Chandra Chatterjee vs Pramatha Nath Chatterjee reported in IC Vol. LXII! 758 it has been held that, "The landlord's undertaking for enjoyment by the tenant is implied from the relationship of landlord and tenant. [Transfer of Property Act, section 108 (c) Budd Scott vs Daniel (2), Markham vs Pagett (1)) and the undertaking would include the protection of the tenant from disturbance by the strangers claiming by title paramount." A similar view was taken in Syed Mukhtar Ahmad vs Rani Sunder Koer reported in CWN Vol. XVII Page 960 observing that,
"Sec. 108, Cl.(c) of the Transfer of Property Act is wide enough to include disturbance of possession by a person with a paramount title."
38. Here in the instant Writ Petition, the right to property of the petitioner is infringed by the Respondent No. 8, who purportedly has got a paramount title over the leased property from the person from whom the property was acquired by the Government for RAJUK and in whose favour RAJUK itself has purportedly issued a Clearance Certificate. So the Respondent No. 8 is not a complete stranger or a mere trespasser, rather he is a person claiming through a Clearance Certificate issued by RAJUK or claiming to have a paramount title over the leased property and the disturbance in the possession over the leased property by the Respondent No. 8 is a disturbance that falls within the provisions of section 108(A)(c) of the Transfer of Property Act. Therefore, RAJUK being the landlord and lessor has the obligation to ensure peaceful possession of the petitioner over the leased property by evicting the Respondent No.8 from the said property and putting the petitioner into the possession of the leased property.
39. In this regard, RAJUK further is bound to fulfil its commitment to evict the Respondent No.8 and put the petitioner into the possession of the leased property by operation of the Doctrine of Promissory Estoppel. It is well recognized that this doctrine has evolved by drawing on the notions of equity and justice. Where one party by his words and/or conduct has made to the other party a clear promise, that promise would be binding upon the former who would not be permitted to renege on such promise. Section 115 of the Evidence Act, 1872 comprehensively declares this principle thus:
"115. Estoppel—When one person has, by his declaration, act or omission, intentionally caused or permitted another person to believe a thing to be true and to act upon such belief, neither he nor his representative shall be allowed, in any suit or proceeding between himself and such person or his representative, to deny the truth of that thing."
40. Accordingly, in Cab Express (BD) Ltd vs Commissioner of Customs reported in 9 BLC 398 (Para 17 & 18) it has been observed that, "So it appears that the doctrine of promissory estoppel operates when one of the parties in reliance of the promise made by the other party acts to his detriment and in such case the other party should not be allowed to go back from his promise as the same would cause injustice on the party relying upon the said promise." A similar view was taken in Asaf Khan vs Court of Settlement reported in 8 BLC 1.
41. The High Court Division in Sharping Matshajibi Samabaya Samity Ltd. vs Bangladesh reported in 1982 BLD (HCD) 189 (Para 8) has observed that a promisee, acting in reliance on the promise, if suffers any detriment and alters his position and subsequently the promisor goes back on his promise the same is enforceable in writ jurisdiction. It is stated that where the government makes a promise knowing that it would be acted upon by the promisee and, in fact, the promisee acting in reliance alters his position, the government would be held bound by the promise and the promisee would be entitled to enforce the promise against the government. It has further been held that it is elementary in a republican government that the rule of law is supreme and no one, howsoever high or low is above the law. Everyone is subject to the law fully and completely as any other and the government is no exception. It is indeed the basis of constitutional democracy and rule of law that the government stands on the same footing as a private individual so far as the obligation of the law is concerned, the former is equally bound as the latter. The government cannot claim to be immune from the applicability of the rule of promissory estoppel and repudiate a promise made by it on the ground that such promise fetters its future executive action. If the government does not want its freedom of executive action to be hampered or restricted, the government need not make a promise knowing or intending that it would be acted on by the promisee and the promisee would alter his position relying upon it. But if the government makes such a promise and the promisee acts in reliance upon it and alters its position, there is no reason why the government should not be compelled to make good such promise like any other private individual. In the instant facts and circumstances, this Court finds this reasoning on the applicability of the Doctrine of Promissory Estoppel to be unqualifiedly securing the present petitioner from the adverse consequences of the erratic conduct of RAJUK.
42. In Collector of Customs Chittagong vs A. Hannan reported in 42 DLR (AD) 167 (Para 20 & 21) the Appellate Division has accepted the observations made in Gujarat State Financial Corporation vs M/s Lorus Hotels Pvt. Ltd. reported in AIR 1983 SC 848 that the principle of Promissory Estoppel would certainly estop the Corporation from backing out of its obligation arising from a solemn promise made to another party who acting upon such promise incurred huge expenditure and if the corporation in the fact was not held to his promise the other party would be put in a very disadvantages position.
43. We note that section 108(A)(b) states that the lessor at the request of the lessee shall put him in the possession of the leased property and section 108(A)(c) states that the lessor shall ensure peaceful possession of the lessee over the leased property. In the instant case, the petitioner after being dispossessed by the Respondent No. 8 filed an application before RAJUK for eviction of the Respondent No.8 and to put her into the possession over the leased property. RAJUK after receiving the application internally discussed the issue, sought legal advice from its legal counsel and directed the petitioner to deposit Taka 70,000 and after receiving such direction from RAJUK the petitioner deposited Taka 70,000 to RAJUK. Thereafter, RAJUK initiated proceedings for eviction of the Respondent No. 8 from the leased property, but suddenly backed off from such eviction proceedings without assigning any reasons. As RAJUK by its own action has promised the petitioner to evict the Respondent No. 8 from the leased property and to put her into the possession of the leased property, we find that it is now bound by such promise by operation of the Doctrine of Promissory Estoppel.
44. It is noted that the Respondent No. 8 was added a respondent after issuance of the Rule and, accordingly, notice was duly issued upon the Respondent. However, the Respondent No.8 has not appeared and not contested the Rule. But the petitioner found existence of two Registered Deeds in favour of the Respondent No. 8 and a Clearance Certificate issued by RAJUK in favour of the Respondent No.8 which are detrimental to her interest and are required to be controverted. Accordingly, the petitioner brought the aforesaid documents on record by way of a Supplementary Affidavit.
45. Upon a consideration of the above, it is evident that the said property along with other properties were acquired on 23-12-1964 government for RAJUK (then DIT) under LA Case No. 10/63-64. After a considerable lapse of time, upon application of some aggrieved persons an order of derequisition was passed in the said LA Case on 31-3-1977 only to be revised on 10-9-1977 by the Final Requisition Order. Writ Petition No. 835 of 1977 was filed against the Final Requisition Order and by a resultant judgment of 12-7-1979 the High Court Division effectively restored the derequisition order of 31-3-1977. That led the Ministry of Land on 8-2-1999 to issue a notice directing the District Commissioner, Dhaka to cancel the proceedings of LA Case No. 10/63-64 and subsequently the Official Gazette Notification in evidence of such derequisition was issued on 11-11-1999. Subsequent challenges mounted against the judgment in Writ Petition No. 835 of 1977 in the form of Review Petition No. 13 of 1999, a CPLA arising out of the RevieW Petition both proved to be futile in upholding the validity of the Final Requisition Order of 10-9-1977. The Respondent No. 8, Mr Abdus Salam Mazumder consequentially had secured the Registered Deeds of 25-10-2004 and 1-11-2004 and obtained a Clearance Certificate from RAJUK on 2-10-2007 in circumstances recorded hereinabove. The said Registered Deeds were executed as the direct consequence of the Gazette Notification dated 11-11-1999 for derequisition of the said property.
46. It was now the turn for the derequisition order of 11-11-1999 to face a constitutional challenge from RAJUK in the form of Writ Petition No.5198 of 2003 along with several Writ Petitions filed against the same by others. After hearing the Writ Petitions, the High Court Division predicated on the rationes decidendi of a catenae of cases reported in 44 DLR (AD) 260, 3 MLR (AD) 91, 52 DLR 125, 52 DLR (AD) 176, 9 MLR (AD) 151, 46 DLR 205 and 50 DLR (AD) /I and made the Rule absolute by a Judgment and Order dated 15-11-2007 as found that given the provision of law and the decisions as referred to the entire purported derequisition exercise effected through memos and notifications issued by the Ministry of Land are illegal, mala fide and made without lawful authority and, therefore, shorn of any legal effect. In setting aside the Gazette Notification of 11-11-1999, that Court further ordered that,
"All actions taken pursuant to the said notifications are also declared to have been taken without lawful authority and of no legal effect."
47. After frequent queries no information has been found about any appeal filed against the aforesaid Judgment and Order and RAJUK also did not find any existence of such appeal. Therefore, it leads this Court to conclude that the aforesaid Judgment and Order are final and binding and as per the aforesaid Judgment all actions taken including the execution of the Registered Deeds and issuance of Clearance Certificate pursuant to the Official Gazette Notification as to derequisition of the said property are illegal and the petitioner need not at this juncture seek any further declaration to that effect.
<u>48. That being the case, we find that the purported execution of the Registered Deeds and the issuance of the Clearance Certificate neither create any legal right in favour of the Respondent No.8 nor provide any excuses for RAJUK not to comply with its earlier promise to evict the Respondent No.8 from the leased property and restore the petitioner's possession of the same.</u>
49. Upon a consideration further of the facts and grounds on issues of both maintainability as well as the issue of the conflicting rights of parties stemming from LA Case No. 10 of 1963-64 and going through the various twists and turns concerning derequisition and the rights that were created subsequently leading to the judgment in particular in Writ Petition No. 5198 of 2003, we are inclined to find merit in the Application and substance in the Rule issued.
Resultantly, the Rule is made absolute with the direction below.
50. The petitioner being led down the garden path by RAJUK and left high and dry abruptly, it is consequentially incumbent upon RAJUK to revive the stalled process of eviction of the trespasser from the case/leased property within the period of 6(six) weeks from the date of receipt of a certified copy of this Judgment and Order. It shall thereafter be incumbent upon RAJUK as lessor to ensure the Petitioner lessee's full possession and enjoyment of the said property and to facilitate the completion of all matters outstanding pertaining to the said property to the benefit of the Petitioner lessee.
51. There is no Order as to costs.
Communicate this Judgment and Order at once.
End.

full_judgment:
This Rule was issued calling upon the opposite party No.1 to show cause as to why the impugned judgment and order dated 22-5-2007 passed by the learned Joint District Judge, 1st Court, Sirajgonj in Miscellaneous Appeal No. 18 of 2003 allowing the appeal and setting-aside the judgment and order dated 20-3-2003 passed by the learned Senior Assistant Judge, Sadar, Sirajgonj in Miscellaneous Case No. 31 of 1999 allowing the pre-emption should not be set-aside and/or such other or further order or orders passed as to this Court may seem fit and proper.
2. Relevant facts, in short, are that the petitioner Md Sohrab Ali Sheikh as pre-emptor filed Miscellaneous Case (pre-emption) No. 31 of 1999 before the learned Senior Assistant Judge, Sadar, Sirajgonj for pre-empting the case land as described in the schedule of the pre-emption application on the allegation that pre-emptor is a co-sharer by purchase in the case holding. The opposite party No.2 sold the case land to the opposite party No.1 by registered kabala dated 11-10-1999 under the camouflage an exchange deed collusively and secretly on 11-10-1999 to defeat the right of pre-emption, the case land is adjacent to chatal land of his rice mill of the pre-emptor, who has been possessing the case land for a long period taking consent brother's wife of seller opposite party No.2; the pre-emptor badly needed the case land. On 24-10-1999, the opposite party No.1 along with 50/60 persons came to the case land and claimed owner of the case land by purchase and asked the pre-emptor to hand over possession of the case land. Thereafter, the pre-emptor obtained certified copy of the impugned deed on 31-10-1999 and came to know definitely about the transfer in question and filed this case for pre-emption depositing consideration money.
3. The opposite party No.1 contested case by filing written statement denying all the material allegations made in the pre-emption application contending, inter-alia, that the opposite party No.1 was owner and possessor of the "ka" schedule land and opposite party No.2 was the owner and possessor of "kha" schedule land of the deed under pre-emption and both of them agreed to exchange their respective land and accordingly, executed and registered an exchange deed and delivered possession and accordingly they have been possessing their exchanged land, the deed No. 7568 dated 31-10-1999 filed by the pre-emptor is forged and without consideration, opposite party No.2 did not execute the same and, as such, the pre-emption case is liable to be rejected.
4. During trial the pre-emptor examined 4 witnesses and the pre-emptee opposite parties examined 2 witnesses.
5. The learned trial Judge after hearing the parties and on considering the materials on record by his judgment and order dated 20-3-2003 allowed the pre-emption on the finding that the pre-emptees could not prove that the deed in question is an exchange deed.
6. On appeal, being Miscellaneous Appeal No. 18 of 2003 the learned Joint District Judge, 1st Court, Serajgonj by the impugned judgment and order dated 22-5-2007 allowed the appeal and set-aside the judgment and order of the trial Court on the finding that the pre-emptor is not co-sharer to the case jote inasmuch as the case joma has been separated and, as such, the pre-emptor is not entitled to get the land under pre-emption.
7. Aggrieved thereby, the pre-emptor-petitioner has come before this Court and obtained the present Rule.
8. Mr Mainul Islam with Mr Md Raju Mia, the learned Advocate appearing for the pre-emptor-petitioner submits that admittedly, the pre-emptor filed the case for preemption on the ground that he is a co-sharer to the case jote by purchase and on this point the pre-emptee-opposite party did not raise any question before the trial Court and it is on record that in the trial Court the pre-emptee opposite party raised only the question i.e. the deed in question is an exchange deed and no pre-emption lies against the exchange deed and the trial Court on considering the evidence and materials on record both oral and documentary held that the deed in question is out and out sale deed and the pre-emptee could not prove that the disputed deed is an exchange deed and on this finding allowed the pre-emption case. The learned Advocate further submits that the pre-emptee after being unsuccessful in the trial Court preferred an appeal and during pendency of the appeal the pre-emptee purchaser filed an application for additional written statements taking a new ground that the pre-emptor is not a co-sharer to the case jote and the Court of appeal below allowed the prayer for additional written statements and the learned Judge of the appellate Court below after hearing the appeal allowed the appeal on the ground that the pre-emptor is not a co-sharer as the joma has been separated long before although there is no specific evidence and materials on record that the joma has been separated and thus, the pre-emptor's co-sharer ship having been ceased. Finally, the learned Advocate submits that the impugned judgment is not based on proper appreciation of the evidence and materials on record inasmuch as the pre-emptee after being unsuccessful in his first plea that the pre-emptor in order to defeat the right of pre-emption executed a sale deed under the camouflage of exchange deed and during appellate stage pre-emptee took a new plea that the pre-emptor is not a co-sharer to the case holding on the ground that the co-sharer ship of the pre-emptor has been ceased long before without any clear and corroborative evidence as to cease of co-sharer ship. Finally, the learned Advocate referring 2 decisions reported in 8 LM (AD) 244 and 1983 BLD (AD) 105 submits that admittedly the petitioner was a co-sharer by purchase and this fact is not denied, mere separation of jama is not the separation of the holding and because of the separation of the jama, the co-sharer ship of the pre-emptor had not been lost and it remained as a co-sharer in the case holding. More so, the pre-emptor is also a contiguous land owner of the case land, its locus-standi to pray for pre-emption of the case land cannot be questioned.
9. Mr Md Zahedul Bari, the learned Advocate appearing for the pre-emptee-opposite party, on the other hand, opposes the Rule and supports the impugned judgment, which was according to him just, correct and proper. He submits that the Court of appeal below rightly held that pre-emptor is not a co-sharer to the case jote as his co-sharer ship has been ceased long before. However, on a query from the Court the learned Advocate for the opposite party submits that he does not want to make any argument on the point that the deed in question is an exchange deed.
10. I have heard the submissions of the learned Advocates for both the sides and perused the Civil Revision application, judgments of two courts below and other papers as filed thereto.
11. The legal battle between pre-emptor-petitioner and pre-emptee opposite party centered round the question of co-sharer ship of the pre-emptor-petitioner. Both the parties adduced evidence in support of their respective cases. The pre-emptor examined 4 witnesses and the pre-emptee examined 2 witnesses. Now, let me advert to the evidence of PWs and OPWs for having a better view of the dispute in question.
12. PW 1 (pre-emptor) stated in his deposition that—
“আমি নালিশী জোতে সূত্রে শরীক” This witness in his evidence also stated that—“আমি ২নং প্রতিপক্ষ কর্তৃক জমি ফেরত দেয়ার গত ইং ৩১-১০-৯৯ তারিখে ৭৫৬৮ নং কবলায় জাবেদা নকল দাখিল করলাম প্রদঃ ২(ক) (আপত্তি) নালিশী দাগের জমিতে আমার মিল থাকার সমর্থনে food license এর কপি দাখিল করলাম ।” This witness in his deposition also stated that he has chatal (rice floor) on the suit land. PW 2 stated in his deposition that— “আমি ২ পক্ষকে চিনি। নালিশী জমি চিনি। নালিশী জমির পার্খে মুক্তিযোদ্ধা অফিস, আমি সে অফিসের কমান্ডার । নালিশী জমির মধ্যে প্রার্থীর চাতাল আছে ।
13. On an analysis of the above quoted evidence, it appears that pre-emptor himself claimed that he is co-sharer to the case land and the pre-emptor has been possessing the case land.
14. On close perusal of the evidence of OPW 1 and OPW 2, it appears that OPWs in their respective evidence stated nothing as to the fact that the pre-emptor is not a co-sharer in the case holding. Besides, the pre-emptee in his written statement stated nothing that pre-emptor is not co-sharer in the case holding. During pendency of the appeal the pre-emptee purchaser for the first time by filing additional written objection incorporated the fact that the pre-emptor is not co-sharer in the case jote as his co-sharer ship has been ceased long before due to separation of joma and in this connection pre-emptee purchaser also adduced oral evidence. It is found that the Court of appeal below allowed the appeal and set-aside the judgment in respect of allowing pre-emption holding that—
“ক্রেতা ১নং প্রতিপক্ষ নিম্নদালতের তথা মূল আপত্তিতে প্রার্থী নালিশী জোতে সহ শরিক কিনা তদ্বিষয়ে কিছুই উল্লেখ না করলেও অন্র আপীল আদালতে অতিরিক্ত আপত্তি দায়েরক্রমে দাবি করে যে প্রারথগণের পূর্ববর্তী শামস উদ্দিন খন্দকার ও আঃ জলিল খন্দকার নালিশী দাগের ২ শতক জমি ক্রয় করে ১৯৮৩/৮৪ সনে ৪৭৩ নং নামজারী মামলা মূলে পৃথক জমাখারিজ করে দখলে থাকাবস্থায় ১৯৯০ সনে প্রার্থীর নিকট বিক্রয় করে দখল দিতে প্রার্থী ১৯৯০/৯১ সনের ১২৪০ নং নামজারী মামলা মূলে ১৩৯০ নং হোল্ডিং খুলে পৃথকভাবে খাজনাদি আদায়ে দখলকার আছে বিধায় প্রার্থী নালিশী জোতে সহ শরিক নহে।”
15. On a close perusal of the evidence of PWs and OPWs together with the pre-emption application and other documents, it appears to me that the pre-emptor has been continuing his chatal business on the case land and in this way he has been owning and possessing the case land. Furthermore, on scrutiny of the record, I do not find any clear or specific evidence on record which suggests that the pre-emptor is not a co-sharer in the case holding.
16. In the case of. Joynal Abedin Molla vs Attar Rahman and others reported in 1983 BLD (AD) 105 wherein it has been held that:
"The respondents were co-sharers, by purchase. This fact is not denied. The document sought to be pre-empted is the CS khatian and SS plots. The pre-emption case could not be refused on the ground that a sub-tenancy has been recorded in SA khatian".
17. In the case of Md Atiqur Rahman Chowdhury and others vs M/s Marshu Ltd. and others reported in 8 LM (AD) 244, it has been held that—
"It further appears that on the basis of the comments of the Tahsilder, Dandkandi Tahsil Office, the Circle Officer (Revenue), Dandkandi, allowed the prayer of the pre-emptor and eventually, the pre-emptor's name was mutated. And accordingly, the pre-emptor started paying rents separately. So factually and legally, there was no separation or sub-division of the case holding but separation of jama only to pay the rent. But both the learned Senior Assistant Judge and the learned Additional District Judge without considering the relevant provisions of law and the mutation proceedings initiated by the concerned Tahsilder and the order of the Circle Officer (Revenue), Dandkandi treated the separation of jama as separation of the case holding and held erroneously that there was separation or sub-division of the case holding and thus the pre-emptor ceased to be a co-sharer in the case holding and therefore, it was not entitled to pray for pre-emption of the case land as a co-sharer in the case holding. However, both the Courts below found that the pre-emptor was a contiguous land owner to the case land."
<u>18. On a reading of the above quoted decisions, I find a clear view of law as it stands today that the petitioner separated joma by way of mutation in its name only. to facilitate the payment of rent and such separation of joma could not be treated as a separation or sub-division of the case holding and it remained to be co-sharer in the case holding. In the facts of the case and for the reasons stated above vis-a-vis the decisions reported in 1983 BLD (AD) 105 and 8 LM (AD) 244, I am clearly of the opinion that the learned Judge of the appellate court below acted illegally in holding that the pre-emptor is not a co-sharer in the case holding as his co-sharer ship has been ceased long before due to separation of joma. More so, the pre-emptor is also a contiguous land owner of the case land, its locus-standi to pray for pre-emption of the case land cannot be questioned.</u>
19. Since, on a query from the Court the learned Advocate for the opposite party submits that he does not want to make any argument as to the point that the deed in question is an exchange deed, it is needless to go into that point whether the impugned deed is an exchange deed.
20. In view of my discussions made in the forgoing paragraphs it is by now clear that the instant Rule must succeed.
21. In the result, the Rule is made Absolute without any order as to costs. The impugned judgment and order dated 22-5-2007 passed by the learned Joint District Judge, 1st Court, Sirajgonj in Miscellaneous Appeal No. 18 of 2003 is set-aside and that the judgment and order of the trial Court dated 20-3-2003 passed in Miscellaneous Case No. 31 of 1999 is hereby restored. The order of stay granted earlier by this Court stands vacated.
Let a copy of this judgment along with lower Courts' record be sent down at once.
End.

full_judgment:
This Rule has. been issued calling upon the Opposite Party No. 1 to show cause as to why the impugned judgment and order dated 22-9-2005, passed by the District Judge, Joypurhat, in Miscellaneous Appeal No.10 of 2000, dismissing the appeal and thereby affirming the judgment and order dated 5-7-2000, passed by the Senior Assistant Judge, Joypurhat, in Pre-emption Miscellaneous Case No.47 of 1983, should not be set-aside and/or pass such other order or further order or orders as to this Court may seem fit and proper.
2. Facts, relevant for disposal of the Rule, in short, are that, one Md Nazrul Islam, as petitioner (plaintiff), had filed Pre-emption Miscellaneous Cise No.47 of 1983, on 10-5-1983, before the court of the then Munsif, Joypurhat, Bogura (now Senior Assistant Judge, Joypurhat), under the provision of section 96 of the State Acquisition and Tenancy Act (SAT), 1950, against Md Majibur Rahman and others, seeking right of pre-emption in respect of the suit property mentioned in the schedule to the petition for pre-emption. The contention of the pre-emptor is that, he is the co-sharer by inheritance and the opposite parties No. 1-4 are strangers in the suit property and that the transfer deed No. 4932 dated 21-4-1983 was executed by pre-emptee No. 5 (seller) in favour of the pre-emptee opposite parties No. 1- 4 (purchasers), without their knowledge and, that, since he is co-sharer in the suit property, therefore, he is entitled to a decree for pre-emption as prayed for.
3. The opposite parties No. 1- 4 contested in the suit by filing written objection denying all material allegations made in the petition for pre-emption. They have also stated that, the pre-emptor is not a co-sharer in the suit property and that the suit was barred by limitation. It has also been asserted that, the sale of the property was negotiated in presence of the pre-emptor and the deed No. 4932 dated 21-4-1983 was executed with his knowledge, since he was not interested to purchase the same. It has further been stated that, the pre-emptees have developed the suit property and have been occupying the same since their purchase and that the necessary parties were not included in this case. Hence, this pre-emption case is liable to be dismissed.
4. The pre-emptor-petitioner deposed himself as PW 1 and produced another witness PW No. 2 in support of his case. The pre-emptor had also produced certain documents which were not at all legible, though marked as Exhibit 1 series and 2. The pre-emptee (defendant) has examined (two) witnesses namely, OPW Nos. 1 and 2 and had also proved the DCR dated 19-2-1984 Exhibit "Ka", CS Khatian No. 402 of Mouza Dharoki, marked as Exhibit "Kha", and also the deed No. 4932 dated 21-4-1982 Exhibit "Ga".
5. The trial court, after hearing the parties and having assessed the evidence on record, by its judgment and order dated 7-5-2000, has allowed the Pre-emption Miscellaneous Case No.47 of 1983. Against the said judgment and order dated 7-5-2000, the pre-emptee (purchasers), as appellants, has preferred Miscellaneous Appeal No.10 of 2000, before the District Judge, Joypurhat, who has also dismissed the appeal by affirming the judgment and order of the trial court, vide its judgment and order dated 22-9-2005.
6. Being aggrieved and dissatisfied with the said judgment and order dated 22-9-2005, the pre-emptee-respondents, as petitioners had filed this revisional application under section 115(1) of the Code of Civil Procedure, 1908, and obtained the present Rule.
7. No one appears either to press the Rule or to oppose the Rule.
8. I have perused the pleadings of the parties, the pre-emption petition, the memo of appeal and the judgments and orders of both the courts below and other materials on record maintained in the LCR.
9. The trial court has framed issue No. 3 as to whether the suit was barred by limitation. The finding of the trial court, as regards this issue, is that, “অত্র মোকদ্দমাটি বিষয়ে ও তথা নালিশী কবলা দলিলটি বিষয়ে জানিবার ৪ (চার) মাস সময়মধ্যে প্রার্থকপক্ষ অত্র অগ্রক্রয় মোকদ্দমা আনয়ন করিয়াছেন। সেহেতু অত্র মোকদ্দমাটি ৯৬(১) উপ-ধারার বিধান অনুযায়ী তামাদি বারিত নহে। এতদরুপ আলোচনা এবং পর্যালোচনার আলোকে আলোচিত ১-৩নং ইস্যুত্রয় প্রার্থক পদের অনুকুলে নিষ্পত্তি হইল।” Thus, the trial court has opined that, the pre-emption case has been filed within 4(four) months from the date of knowledge from 21-4-1982. Therefore, the case was not barred by limitation.
10. Having examined the record of this case, I do not find any evidence as to how or when the pre-emptor has achieved the knowledge of the deed or through whom. Then, having perused the deposition of PW 1 and 2, I do not find any specific date of acquiring knowledge, by the pre-emptor, about the deed No. 4932 dated 21-4-1982. Hence, no specific date could mentioned, by the trial court, from which it had counted the 4 (four) months period to support it's finding that pre-emption case was not barred by limitation.
11. It is to be noted here that, the act of sale or transfer of land is not a secret or illegal act. The transfer of land is not a prohibited deal as are the cases of drugs or illegal arms. Usually, in the case of transfer of land or immovable property in village and in mufassil area, the seller and purchaser sits in several sessions, take measurement of the property in the broad daylight, engage brokers, negotiate the price with more than one buyers, procure and verify the relevant documents, consult lawyer and deed writer, purchase stamp and do so many things that make the deal.
12. Therefore, the mere denial of know-ledge of the sale deed will not suffice. A very strong proof is required to uphold a case that the pre-emptor had no knowledge of the impugned sale. Moreso, when a right of pre-emption tends to abridges the fundamental rights to property guaranteed under Article 42 of the Constitution of the People's Republic of Bangladesh.
13. Rahter, the presumption of knowledge shall be attributed to the pre-emptors and he or she must prove that the suit was not barred by limitation. In some cases, it has been found that, the sellers transferred their land either for money to go abroad or to meet other urgent need. Then, after a few months, they come up-with a story that his brother or uncle had sold the property without his/her knowledge, although in maximum cases the property was sold in their presence or with their knowledge. The courts must keep in mind that the purchasers have purchased the land, not the litigation.
<u>14. In this case, the pre-emptees has specifically stated in their written objection and had testified that, the pre-emptor was aware about the sale from the very beginning and he was mediator. On this point, the pre-eemptor did not adduce any evidence as to how or from whom he got the knowledge of the impugned transfer. On the other hand, the question of limitation has been specifically pleaded in the written objection. Besides, section 3(3) of the Limitation Act, 1908, imposes a statutory duty on the court to frame and decide the issue of limitation, whether it has been pleaded or not by any of the parties of the proceeding.</u>
<u>15. But, in this case although the issue No. 3 as regards the limitation, however, the trial courts finding is not based on any evidence, nor any date of knowledge has been recorded in finding of the trial court, to justify the finding, that this pre-emption case was filed within 4(four) months from the date of knowledge.</u>
<u>16. The pre-emptor has failed to prove that he has filed this case within the statutory period of limitation.</u>
17. The appellate court did not at all frame, nor discussed, the issue of limitation. Indeed, the appellate court did not at all discuss any evidence, nor it had arrived at any independent finding of its own which was obligatory on the part of the appellate court as the last court of fact. The relevant portion of the judgment of the appellate court is as follows:-
“১) জয়পুরহাট সদর সিনিয়র সরকারী জজ আদালতের ৪৭/৮৩ নং প্রিয়েমশন মামলার বিগত ইং ৫-৭-২০০০ তারিখের রায় ও আদেশ রহিত হইতে পারে কিনা?
২) আপীলকারী প্রতিপক্ষের বরাবরে এই আপিলটি মঞ্জুর হইতে পারে কি না?
আলোচনা ও সিদ্ধান্ত
আলোচনার সুবিধার জন্য বিচার্য বিষয় ২টি একত্রে লওয়া হইল ।
মূল প্রিয়েমশন মামলাটি ১৯৮৩ সনে দায়ের করা হইয়াছিল । দীর্ঘ ২২ বছরের মধ্যে পক্ষগণ এই মামলাটি নিষ্পত্তি করিতে পারে নাই। মূল মামলার আদেশ নামা পর্যালোচনা করিয়া এই আপীল আদালতের ধারণা জন্নিয়াছে যে, কোন পক্ষই মামলাটি দ্রুত নিষ্পত্তিতে আগ্রহী নয় । একটি প্রিয়েমশন মামলা নিষ্পত্তি হইতে ২২ বছর সময় লাগে কিভাবে? এই আপীলটি ও শুনানী করিতে কোন পক্ষই আগ্রহ প্রকাশ করেন নাই। এই আপীল শুনানী আপীলকারী কিভাবে প্রতিবন্ধকতা সৃষ্টি করিয়াছে তাহা এই আপীল আদালতের গত ১৯-৯-২০০৫ ইং তারিখে আদেশ বিস্তারিত বর্ণনা করা হইয়াছে।
গত ১৪-৯-২০০৫ ইং তারিখ আপীলকারী আপীল আদালত জোর পূর্বক আপীলকারীর নিকট থেকে ৩/৪ মিনিটের বক্তব্য আদায় করিয়া মামলাটি পরবর্তী শুনানীর জন্য ধার্য করিলে, আপীলকারী আর শুনানী করে নাই। রেসপনডেন্ট পক্ষ ও অতি সংক্ষিপ্ত বক্তব্য রাখিয়া দাবী করিয়াছেন নিম্ন আদালতের ৫-৯-২০০০ ইং তারিখের রায় সঠিক হইয়াছে। বিধায় আপীল নামঞ্জুর হইবে।
আপীলের মেমোতে আপীলকারী প্রতিপক্ষগণের মূল বক্তব্যই হইল, নিম্ন আদালতে পক্ষদোষের ব্যাপারে সুস্পষ্ট সিদ্ধান্ত দেয় নাই এবং জমা ভাগের মাধ্যমে প্রার্থী ন���রুল ইসলাম নালিশী জোতে সহ অংশীদার না থাকা সত নিম্ন আদালত ৫-৭-২০০০ ইং তারিখে রায়ে প্রার্থী নজরুল ইসলামের বরাবরে প্রিয়েমশন মামলাটি মঞ্তুর করিয়াছেন ।
আপীলকারী প্রতিপক্ষগণ দীর্ঘ ২২ বছরের মধ্যেও প্রয়োজনীয় কাগজপত্র এবং সাক্ষ্য প্রমাণের মাধ্যমে প্রমাণ করিতে পারে নাই যে, নালিশী ভূমি জমাভাগের মাধ্যমে পৃথক খতিয়ান হওয়ার কারণে প্রার্থী নজরুল ইসলাম প্রিয়েমশনের অধিকার থেকে বঞ্চিত হইয়াছেন ।
নিম্ন আদালতের তর্কিত রায় পর্যালোচনা করা হইল । তর্কিত রায়ে কোন গুরুতর অনিয়ম পরিলক্ষিত হয় নাই । পক্ষগণ মনযোগের সহিত শুনানী করিলে এই আদালত নিম্ন আদালতের রায়ে কোথায় ভুল-ক্রুটি আছে সে ব্যাপারে আরো সম্যক ধারণা পাইত।
দীর্ঘ বিচারাধীন এই প্রিয়েমশন মামলার তর্কিত রায়ে হস্তক্ষেপ করা হইতে এই আপীল আদালত বিরত থাকিতেছে। সার্বিক বিবেচনার তর্কিত রায় বহাল পূর্বক এই আপীলটি নামঞ্জুর করার সিদ্ধান্ত লওয়া হইতেছে।
অতএব,
আদেশ হয়
দোতরফাভাবে এই আপীলটি নামঞ্জুর করা হইল । জয়পুরহাট সদর সিনিয়র সহকারী জজ আদালতের ৪৭/৮৩ নং প্রিয়েমশন মামলার বিগত ইং ৫-৭-২০০০ তারিখের রায় বহাল রাখা হইল । অত্র রায়ের অনুলিপি সহ নিন্ন আদালতের নথি ফেরত প্রদান করা হউক ।
স্বাক্ষর/নরেন্দ্র চন্দ্র দাশ
জেলা জজ, জয়পুরহাট ।
তারিখঃ ২২-৯-২০০৫।
18. This judgment of the appellate court is abhorrent to the judicial norms and functions. In the judgment of the appellate court, I find no discussion of any oral or documentary evidence, nor any independent finding arrived at by it on any relevant issue. Indeed, there is no finding arrived at by the appellate court. Therefore, this cannot be a case of concurrent finding in that the appellate court has recorded no finding.
19. Having read the judgment of the trial court, I do not find any discussion, nor finding that the pre-emptors are co-sharers of the CS recorded owners. Although, it has been recorded that, “দাখিলী সি,এস,এম,আর,আর খতিয়ান দৃষ্টে প্রমাণিত হয় যে, প্রার্থক নালিশী জোতে উত্তরাধিকারী সুন্রে শরীক।”But, there is no discussion in the judgment as to who are the CS and MRR recorded owners and how the pre-emptors are related to them. The court must arrive at specific findings clearly showing the basis and the accrual of the right of pre-emption, moreover, when the pre-emptee has specifically stated in their written objection that, the pre-emptor is not co-sharer in the suit property.
20. In our court, a huge matter, arising out the pre-emption cases are comprising a large share of backlogs of this Court. Many of these cases are filed for attaining unlawful gain by the pre-emptors, moreso, after a long delay and on false claim that the pre-emptors were not aware of the transfer in question.
21. In view of the foregoing discussion, I find merit in this Rule and accordingly, the Rule should be made absolute.
Order
In the result, the Rule is made absolute.
The impugned judgment and order dated 22-9-2005, passed by the District Judge, Joypurhat, in Miscellaneous Appeal No.10 of 2000, dismissing the appeal and thereby affirming the judgment and order dated 5-7-2000, passed by the Senior Assistant Judge, Joypurhat, in Pre-emption Miscellaneous Case No.47 of 1983, is hereby set-aside. The order of stay granted earlier by this Court is hereby vacated.
No costs.
